speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. GARLAND (Bow River) moved:
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
That the interim and final reports respectively of the Hon. Mr. Justice Clarke, commissioner appointed to inquire into the alleged existence of corrupt or illegal practices in the election held in the electoral district of Athabaska, in the province of Alberta, on the 29th of October, 1925, which reports were laid on the table of the house on December 15, 1926, be referred to the select standing committee on privileges and elections.
He said:	It may be proper at this stage
that I should survey briefly the incidents that have led up to this motion. On March 18, 1926, as the result of a petition from electors in the district of Athabaska, this house passed a motion approving the appointment of a commissioner to conduct an investigation into the alleged fraud, corruption, perjury, forgery, ballot-stuffing and other misdemeanours that took place during that election. The Hon. Mr. Justice Clarke, a reputable and well known member of the bench, was appointed
179S	COMMONS
Athabaska Election-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
on July 10, 1926, to undertake the investigation. Mr. Justice Clarke submitted two reports, an interim and a final. The interim report included statements or allegations that corrupt and illegal practices had extensively prevailed, and specifically designated a large number of polls, twelve or more, where stuffing of ballot boxes and the forging of returns and other documents had occurred. The report, however, contained no specific recommendation to the government; it simply presented the finding. This and the final report have never been considered by parliament nor acted upon.
Surely it is the duty of members of this house to protect the rights and privileges of the people of this country during elections. It certainly is not our duty to evade our responsibility in preventing, so far as we can, a recurrence of the sort of thing that prevailed so extensively in Athabaska. I have no hesitation in declaring to you, Mr. Speaker, that in my opinion the very existence of democracy itself and the continuance of responsible government in this country will depend entirely upon our determination to stamp out, at its very inception, any attempt at practices of this nature in elections in Canada.
The purpose of this motion is to have these two reports referred to the committee on privileges and elections in order that after a thorough examination of them provision may be made, either by amendments to the Election Act, by amendments to the criminal code, or by amendments in any other direction that may prevent a recurrence of disgusting performances of the kind that took place in Athabaska.
A motion similar to this passed the house on February 15 of last year, but I regret to say the committee never met. I inquired of the clerk of committees recently and found that, from the moment the committee was appointed on February 15 to the end of the session, they -could not secure a quorum. Meetings of the committee were called on March 2, 3, and 8 of last year, and about twelve or thirteen members attended; at that time, however, a quorum of the committee consisted of fifteen. At the request of the members who attended, the chairman introduced a motion into this house on March 8 asking that the quorum be reduced. At first that motion stood over at the request of the then leader of the opposition for further consideration, and no action was taken by the chairman. On March 29, some twenty-one

days later, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Kellner) moved tha-t the quorum be reduced, and although the Minister of Justice objected briefly the motion was adopted. I regret to say that although the quorum was reduced to nine members, still the committee could not hold a meeting.
I am n-ot going to impute motives; I am not going to suggest that this was a deliberately engineered business in order to prevent a discussion of this matter. Frankly, I cannot find it within me to believe that any hon. members of this house or of the government, would consent -for one moment to any such action. Therefore I can only reassure myself by assuming that the reason was the occupation of the members in other committees which were then sitting.
Additional reasons for asking the house to pass the motion will be realized readily when I say that by the report of Mr. Justice Clarke it was found that the returning officer himself could neither write nor read. Think of it, Mr. Speaker; the returning officer for an electoral district of this country unable to write or read. In some cases the registrars refused to send out the voters' lists, and the candidate who contested that constituency from our group had less than 100 of the 235 lists on polling day. Ballots were cast by men who had been long dead; in one case a ballot was cast in the name of a man who had been dead for twelve years, while in another -case a ballot was cast in the name of a man who had been dead three years. Many people voted who had never resided in the district, and in other cases people voted who had resided in the district some several years before, but who had left from three to seven yearn prior to the date of the election. At least three polls were held in a forest reserve, where people were neither living nor permitted to live under the laws of this country. Very briefly,' that is a recitation of some of the reasons why I feel satisfied that this house will pass this motion, in justice to itself and to the people of this country.
On February 15 of last year a fairly representative d-eJbate too-k place on a similar motion, and at that time the Minister of Justice used these words:
I am in favour of the motion, and I may also say that if, as a result of this being referred to the committee on privileges and elections, gQiug way may bs found to prevent electoral corruption as it seems to have prevailed in that election, I and those who sit with me on this side of the house will be only too glad to associate with my hon. friend in that respect.

Athabaska Election-Mr. Spencer
The then leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) said:
If this be so, what is the reason? Has the government taken no action in the matter? Has the government quietly taken the position that having referred the matter to the local Attorney General their duty is at an end?
The hon. gentleman was dealing at that time with the question of the punishment of those who had offended against the electoral and criminal laws in respect of that election. Speaking on behalf of the Conservative party, the hon. member accepted the motion. The Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), who took part in the discussion, said:
A question has been brought before the house by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), and I have no doubt that every member of this house, no matter to which party he may belong, is of the one opinion, and that is that every man who has been implicated in electoral frauds should be prosecuted without mercy, and that justice should prevail.
Further, he went on to say:
In conclusion, when these two reports are laid before the committee on privileges and elections, I believe that every member sitting on that committee will be moved by one common spirit, and that is to try and devise means of preventing any such things happening in the future as were proved to have happened in that constituency in the election of 1925.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), now leader of the opposition, said:
The first matter that should be considered is: What recommendation can the committee make with respect to amending the election laws of this country so as to prevent a repetition of those conditions? The second is also a matter of some importance as it touches the position of the civil servants of this country. Shall a civil servant who has been convicted of a crime or who admits the commission of a crime and has secured immunity by reason of his confession, continue in office?
The reference of the hon. member was to a statement which was made in this house that the government had allowed to continue in office postmasters, land agents and other civil servants who had been found guilty by Mr. Justice Clarke of the most wilful forms of deliberate ballot stuffing, forgery, perjury and fraud in that election. That was the position taken by the hon. member for west Calgary (Mr. Bennett), who went on to say:
Shall the public service acts of this country not be amended so as to provide that by reason of any confession of that character he shall at once vacate his position?
The Prime Minister interjected the remark " surely ", The hon. member for West Calgary then continued:
This house should use its every effort to stop that sort of thing because, if we do not prevent
it, our very democratic institutions are destroyed and responsible government has indeed become valueless in this country. That is the reason that the motion made this afternoon by the hon. member meets with my approval
I have nothing further to say, Mr. Speaker, except that I feel satisfied that the members of this house will come to the same decision with the same unanimity of opinion, to see that the matter is cleaned up as far as it can be cleaned up by a committee of this house.
I feel that they will be as unanimous this year as was the case last year, and I will leave the matter to the house.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I
wish to say a few words in support of the motion which has been made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I do so very willingly, because the election in Athabaska took place in the fair province of Alberta, of which I am very proud to be one of the representatives. Since such things have happened in Athabaska and also in Peace River, outsiders might think that the elections in Alberta are conducted on a very questionable basis, but I want to say to this house that I do not know of any province in this wide Dominion where elections are usually conducted more cleanly than in that province. The districts of Athabaska and Peace River happen to be outlying districts, and certain practices entered into those elections which I hope will be Checked. It is with the hope of cleaning up conditions in the future that we now ask that this report of Mr. Justice Clarke be sent to the committee on privileges and elections.
I am glad to support this motion, because I think a great wrong was done to an hon. gentleman who now sits in this house, who was a member from 1921 to 1925, who did excellent work for this country and for his constituency, and who was prevented by questionable practices from coming back to parliament in 1925. It has been shown very clearly indeed, through the investigation which took place, that had this gentleman been accorded anything like fair treatment, he would have received a big majority in the election of 1925, and would have been returned again. Instead of that someone else took his place. It was well known at the time that conditions in Athabaska were in a very bad state, and that things had occurred of such a character as to cause any self-respecting citizen to blush at the very thought of them. I should like to point out that the hon. member who did come down in 1925 happened to sit on the government side, and there was no demand for an investigation from hon. gentlemen supporting the govern-
1800	COMMONS
Athabaska Election-Mr. Spencer
ment. I am fully convinced, however, that had that member been sitting in any other part of the house, the government would have speedily caused an investigation to be held. Under the circumstances it became the duty of hon. members sitting on this side to support the recommendations and petitions forwarded to Ottawa asking that an investigation be made. With these petitions before the house an investigation was in due course ordered and it took place, first of all under Mr. Justice Beck, and later on under Mr. Justice Clarke. In the course of that investigation revelations of a most amazing characater were made, amongst them incidents like the following:	Many witnesses,
including deputy returning officers, fled the country rather than face justice. Vote plugging became quite general. Cheques were paid on forged endorsations. Some cheques were made out to fictitious officials. A certain poll clerk was appointed who could neither read nor write; and as the hon. member who preceded me said, even the returning officer was in the same extraordinary position. Switching and substitution of ballots was practised. Fictitious polls were held in districts where there were no settlers. Ballot boxes were freely plugged, and so on ad infinitum. In the election of 1926 the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) came back to parliament with a large majority owing to the fact that the investigation had taken place in the meantime. So that there is not the slightest doubt but that the hon. member to whom I refer would not have been kept away previously had there been fair dealing in the constituency of Athabaska.
As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) said, a motion was adopted referring the report of Mr. Justice Clarke to the committee on privileges and elections. The report was referred to that committee but a quorum could not be obtained at any of the meetings, so that it was not considered. I for one am not going to make any charges with respect to those members who did not turn up at the meetings of that committee. I take it for granted that every hon. member here wants to wipe out the disgrace of the reprehensible doings which took place in Athabaska in 1925. I do not suppose there is a single hon. member who is satisfied to permit that blemish on our reputation to remain. I can only say, like my hon. friend who preceded me, that there must have been so many committees sitting at the time that a quorum could not be obtained by the committee on privilege and elections. I therefore earnestly hope that not only will the
fMr. Spencer.]
house vote in favour of the committee on privileges and elections considering this report, but that the members who form that committee will make a point of seeing that a quorum is obtained, that the report is duly considered, and such action taken as will wipe out this disgraceful episode in the political life of Canada.

Referring to the rules of the house, I find on page 234 of Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, standing order 79, bribery and elections, which reads:
If it shall appear that any member hath been elected and returned a member of this house, or endeavoured so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt practices, this house will proceed with the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned in such bribery or other corrupt practices.
The note on that reads:
This standing order has nothing to do with the different laws which fully provide for the trial and punishment of corrupt practices at elections, but it reiterates the house's privilege to deal with offences of bribery and corruption after they have been proved before the competent courts. Where there have been special reports concerning bribery or riots at elections, the conduct of returning officers; undue influence and intimidation; the alteration of the poll, the absence, misconduct or perjury of witnesses; defects or uncertainty in the law; the propriety of suspending the writ; or any other exceptional circumstances-the house lias taken such measures as -were required by law or usage or as appeared suitable to the occasion. It has been usual in such cases to order a copy of the judgment delivered by the judge and the minutes of evidence to be laid before the house.
Not only following out that rule, but calling upon what has often been referred to as the highest court of justice, namely, this house, I think it is within our power to pass the report to the committee on privileges and elections and to have the matter thoroughly threshed out.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the story of the Athabaska election of 1925 is amazing; it is almost incredible in its details of corrupt practices. We are all accustomed to the story of elections being conducted more or less crookedly, with some
buying and selling of votes, some infractions of the Dominion Elections Act, and that sort of thing; with that I do not for the moment propose to deal. There are those in every party who do that sort of thing and I am not saying at the moment that the party to which I belong is any better or any worse than any other. My purpose in addressing the house at this moment is not to deal with that phase of the subject. These matters, peccadilloes, if you like to call them, minor bits of corruption, can be dtealt with under the existing machinery. But the questions that arise from a consideration of the report of the commissioner, Mr. Justice Clarke, are far wider than that.
Briefly, there are two matters which I think we should touch upon. One of them which has already been dealt with by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), is the question of retaining civil servants in the government employ when they have been reported on as having been guilty of corrupt practices during an election, no matter whether they have been by the judge granted immunity or not. The Minister of the Interior seems to believe that there was no such case in connection with this election.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior

If there
was, I am not aware of it. I know that in every case that came to my notice the employee *was promptly dismissed.

speechtext:
If he does become aware
of such a case I am sure he will exercise the proper function and have that man or woman got rid of.	There is, however, a
larger question than that which arises and that is the question of the organization and control of the machinery which has to do with the conduct of elections generally in this country. I cannot forbear from quoting just a line here and there from the report of Mr. Justice Clarke which deals not with the ordinary things that we hear of in elections, such as the buying and selling of votes, or impersonation which I am sure the officers of the law do their best on all occasions to stamp out, but with the larger question of the organization and control of the machinery in connection with elections. He says in regard to Reita lake poll:
I find that what purports to be the voters' list for this poll and to be signed by Thomas J. Cardinal as registrar, and returned with the election papers, contains 73 names, and that not more than ten persons were entitled to vote in this division.
He says further:
I find that the poll book is a forgery as no votes were polled.

Still there was a large majority given in favour of the candidate, Cross, who was declared elected. He says in regard to Bates poll:
The voters' list for this poll certified by Peter Peterson as registrar contains two hundred names. Less than ten voters resided in the polling division, which is a reserve.
In regard to Cushing poll, this is what he says:
No voters' list for this poll can be found.
But an election was carried on and a large majority returned in favour of Mr. Cross, the successful candidate. In regard to this poll he states further:
The poll book indicates that there were 194 names on the voters' list but there appear to have been only four qualified voters in the polling division.
He also states:
In fact no poll was held and no person voted.
In regard to Prairie Lake poll, he says:
There are no qualified voters in this polling division but a voters' list was prepared containing 59 names.
Mr. Cross again got the great majority of these. In regard to Parenteau poll, he says:
The voters list for this poll was manufactured at Harry Bowtell's house and signed as registered by Mrs. Rose A Preece, a sister of Mrs. Harry Bowtell.
_ It never went through the proper proceedings for its initiation and completion. So, as one goes through the list, one finds that all these matters have to do not with the ordinary political corruption as one understands it in reference to an election, but with the organization and preparation by government officials of the preliminaries for an election. There was a stamp which must never leave the registrar's hands, but the registrar was a hundred miles away from where the stamp was. The registrar was at Lac la Biche and the ballots were printed in Edmonton, more than one hundred miles distant. The stamp was sent to Edmonton where somebody used it to stamp the ballots. The commissioner says in regard to Margu poll:
Harris prepared a voters' list the night before the election from the names furnished by Lawler and that constituted the list for this division. It contained 35 names.
At Lac la Biche poll the same thing happened, and so with the others. I will not go through the list, but my point in reciting what the house has already heard is that those are matters which have to do with the functions of the chief electoral officers in
[Mr. Geary.1
getting ready for the holding of an election and preparing the machinery for holding it. The hon. member who now sits for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) was robbed of his seat. He stayed at home during that winter and there came down in his place a man who sat here and voted as a representative of the people of this country whereas he really represented nobody at all. The constituency of Athabaska was not represented during the session of 1926. As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has said, you rob this country of the very essence of responsible government if you allow people to sit on the benches of parliament who do not represent anybody but who, by something that has been allowed to be done perhaps through a fault in the act, are sitting here in fact.
Last year this report was before the government; it was laid on the table of the house. If I remember rightly it came to the Solicitor General on the 19th October and, as was his duty, he sent it forward to the Secretary of State with an intimation that the provincial attorney general be communicated with, with a view to punishing those found guilty. He added at the bottom of his communication in effect:	Make haste in the matter because
my letter being dated the 19th instant, the period of one year allowed by the statute for the prosecution of these offences will expire in ten days. That had to go through the hands of the Secretary of State and out to the government of Alberta, to be acted on within ten days. The delay was not the fault of the Solicitor General; I have no doubt he dealt with the matter as expeditiously as possible; but the government could not have rested with the conviction that it was doing its full duty in forwarding within ten days of the expiration of the time for prosecution of these offences a communication to the attorney general requesting him to . take action. If I make complaint at all of the government in reference to this matter it is this, that it had before it all this material, that it had before it the motion my hon. friend from Bow River has cited which was passed last year referring the matter to the privileges and elections committee, that it had before it the fact that the committee had not met and discussed the matter referred to them, and still, so far as I can learn, the government has not thought it its duty to take the place, so to speak, of the committee, to take into consideration all the facts brought out in the report of Mr. Justice Clarke, and to bring down to this house some initial action of its own in regard to the matter.

Athabaska Election-Mr. Lapointe
If we cannot in some way or other do better in the matter of the control and operation of elections than we did in Athabaska, then the lookout is pretty poor for any one of us, particularly if you do not happen to be a candidate of a government that is in power, with some opportunity to get close to the election machinery, if any one would do such a thing. We have no right to assume that a similar election may not be carried on when this house next goes to the country, and it may be done in, say, ten or twenty constituencies instead of just one. Now is the time, with this instance before us, to take action to prevent the recurrence of practices of this kind. It is not enough merely to punish those who are caught at their evil work, although that is very well, and the more stiffly we punish those who are guilty, the better for all of us and the better for the country. Let them learn once for all that practices of that kind will not be tolerated, and that swift and sure punishment will follow anything of that sort. But these examples lose their effect if they are allowed to sink too far into the past, and the farther away we get from the election and the dimmer the memory of the evil practices in the Athabaska election, the less effect any action taken in regard to it will have. Let us have action taken now. It has been long enough coming, and let us act while the memory of these things is still fresh in the minds particularly of my hon. friends from Alberta. Let us see to it, having this example before us, that some means are devised to bring the election act into harmony with the desire of everybody, that this sort of thing shall not be tolerated any longer in this country.
I entirely agree with the motion, Mr. Speaker. I support it and trust that the government will take so much interest in the committee on privileges and elections that they will with their powers, so to speak, of whip and spur and whatever else they may have in the way of organization or control of committees, not neglect, to see that this matter receive consideration and be properly dealt with, and a report brought in early enough to enable the house to take action upon it during this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I may say immediately, Mr. Speaker, that I have no objection to the motion of my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), and that we on this side of the house will certainly support the reference of this report to the privileges and elections committee, and if as a result of the work of that committee any amendments may be suggested 56103-115
that will have for their effect the improvement of our electoral law, and that will make it more difficult for people who are liable to commit illegal practices at elections to do so, we shall be only too pleased to support any amendments which might be proposed in that regard.
With regard to this particular case, I think it is well that I should state what has actually happened. By chapter 51 of the revised statutes of Canada, parliament adopted an address asking the governor in council to appoint a commissioner to inquire into the existence of any corrupt or illegal practices which might have taken place in that election. Mr. Justice Clarke was finally appointed, and 'he made the investigation which the statute required him to carry out. He made two reports, an interim report and a final report. Under the law he had to report to the Governor General the evidence taken, and what he had found concerning the matter referred to him, and he did so. He had to report the names of all persons whom he found to have been guilty of any corrupt or illegal practices at the election, with the particulars thereof, and he did so. The law, section 30 of chapter 51, provides that:
Every such report shall he submitted to parliament:	(a) within fourteen days after
such report is made, if parliament is sitting at the expiration of the said period of fourteen days; or (h) if parliament is not then sitting, within fourteen days from the time of the next meeting of parliament after such report is made.
The two reports were submitted to parliament according to law.
There is a duty placed upon the Attorney General of Canada under the statutes. Section 31 of chapter 51 provides:
Whenever it appears by the report of the commissioners under this act that any person named by them has been guilty of a corrupt or illegal practice and has not been furnished by them with a certificate of indemnity, such report with the evidence taken by the commissioners, shall be laid before the Attorney General of Canada, who shall, if in his opinion there is sufficient evidence available for a prosecution, certify 'Such opinion to the Secretary of State, who shall thereupon communicate the report with the evidence to the lieutenant governor of the province in which the election wras held.
And section 32 says:
The Attorney General of Canada shall instruct counsel to assist in any prosecution which is thereon instituted by the local authorities charged with the 'administration of justice.
The interim report, the first report, submitted 'by Mr. Justice Clarke, was received by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. REVISED EDITION
1804	COMMONS
Athabaska Election-Mr. Lapointe
Cannon), who was thea acting Attorney Geaeral of Canada, during my absence, I believe, at the Imperial conference. Having read the evideace, the officers of the depart-meat, because, after all, it is a departmental affair, made their report to him, aad he signed the following certificate:
The undersigned has the honour to inform you that the Hon. Mr. Justice Clarke, the commissioner appointed to inquire into the alleged existence of corrupt or illegal practices in the elections holden in the electoral district of Athabaska, in the province of Alberta, on the 29th of October, 1925, has laid before him his interim report, together with the evidence taken by the commissioners upon which such report is based.
The undersigned is of opinion that there is sufficient evidence available for prosecution against William A. Deyl, William (Bill) Lawler, H. M. Barton, and Harry Bowtell, named in the said report, and he hereby certifies such opinion to you accordingly in accordance with the provisions of section 31 of the Corrupt Practices Enquiries Act, revised statutes of Canada, 1906, chapter 8.
It is to be observed that the matter is of some urgency in view of the fact that the time for prosecution expires at the end of one year from the 29th October, 1925. Report and evidence herewith.
Dated at Ottawa, this nineteenth day of October, 1926.
(Sgd.) Lucien Cannon,
Acting Attorney General of Canada.
This was sent to the Secretary of State, as the law provides, and the Secretary of State acknowledged its receipt, and informed my hon. friend that the necessary action had been taken in reference thereto. I find in the record the letter of the secretary to the Lieutenant Governor of Alberta acknowledging receipt of a letter from the attorney general stating that he had taken action and that warrants had been issued against those parties who had not received a certificate of indemnity from the investigating judge. After the final report was received I, as Attorney General of Canada, issued another certificate to the Secretary of State in these terms:
The undersigned is of opinion that there is sufficient evidence available for prosecution against Isaac Gagnon, William A. Deyl, William (Bill) Lawler, H. M. Barton, W. R. Jex and W. E. Proctor, named in the said final report, and he hereby certifies such opinion to you accordingly.
This was sent to the Secretary of State, and he forwarded it with the evidence and other papers which the law requires to the authorities in Alberta.
Now my friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) cited Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms to the effect that the house has the right and authority to proceed against

men who have committed illegal practices at an election. There is no doubt of that. But parliament in its wisdom has decided that the provincial authorities can more effectively deal with such a matter, and it is their duty to do so. I have not the slightest doubt that the local authorities of Alberta have done everything which they could do to prosecute those who were guilty of any illegal practices at that election.
My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary) has just said that if the committee on privileges and elections did not do anything it was the duty of the government to take action. I beg respectfully to say to him that usually the government is charged with doing too much, with trespassing upon the jurisdiction of parliament, and that in this particular instance the law makes it the work of parliament altogether. It is parliament that directs investigation to be made, and the law says the report shall be submitted to parliament. If there is anything to do it is for parliament to decide; and as far as we are concerned, I repeat, we shall be only too pleased to do anything which the committee recommends in that respect. I do not know whether my friend from South Toronto is not himself a member of the privileges and elections committee. Surely he would not suggest that we should do what the law says he himself ought to do in that respect.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: If I may interrupt the hon. Minister of Justice-I merely suggested that failing action by the committee, with all the information contained in this report before the government, they might very well consider it with a view to taking such steps to revise the Elections Act as might seem necessary and wise in the circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I have no doubt that,
although the Elections Act has been revised many times, it may be still further improved, and I for one think that prior to the next general election something might be done in this direction; all the wisdom of parliament might be conscripted for the purpose of devising such amendments as would improve and strengthen the present act in this respect.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Is not this a question of administration rather than of law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
It is really a question
for parliament to decide what would be the best electoral law to prevent frauds.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
But at the present time it is a matter of enforcing the law which you have.

Athabaska Election-Sir Henry Drayton

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Absolutely. But what
had, to be done has been done. I do not know what has been the result of the prosecutions instituted by the province of Alberta. My friends may know better than I do in that respect. We have received no report.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Was the department of the Minister of Justice represented?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I stated in parliament
that we should be only too pleased to appoint counsel to help in any proceedings which might be instituted against those who were charged with fraud and other illegal practices at the election. We never were requested to help and, as I have stated' already, it is for the local authorities to take proceedings. We were advised that they had actually issued warrants against the guilty parties.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend kindly tell the house in how many prosecutions which he initiated in this way he was successful; what were the convictions, and against whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I never initiated any
proceedings in that respect.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: My hon. friend asserted that certain prosecutions had taken place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I assume they
took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I do not know.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I was going to ask my hon. friend if he knew how many convictions had been secured.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I do not know.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: My hon. friend does not know. Can he tell the house how many of those convicted have been let out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I do not know.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
What about Baldy
Robb?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: We have done what the law stated we should do. As Attorney General of Canada I have certified to the Secretary of State the names of those persons whom I thought should be prosecuted. It was not either for me or the Secretary of State to issue warrants; the law provides that those warrants Shall be issued by the provincial authorities. The provincial authorities have acknowledged receipt of our certificate and told us that they were issuing warrants.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is mot giving the house a very good-

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Is it a question?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I thought he was through.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I do not wish to deprive the hon. gentleman of his privilege of asking a question, but I do not think the hon. Minister of Justice has concluded his remarks.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I shall not deprive the
house any longer of the pleasure of listening to my hon. friend, whom we are all so pleased to welcome back. May I add once again that I will support the motion of my hon. friend. I am prepared to help him in any way which might improve the election methods of Canada.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first instance may I thank my hon. friend for his very kindly reference to myself. He is always delightfully amiable and it always affords me great pleasure to have anything to do with him. But, sir, I want to direct the attention of the house to one or two things. Some way and somehow we have had delay in punishing election ciimes that have never yet, so far as I know, been equalled in iniquity in this country. That delay in the first instance was brought about by my hon. friends opposite. The Minister of Justice said:	This is not a
matter for the house, it is a matter for the commissioner to deal with. Why? Because when this house wanted to become seized of this iniquity, when we wanted to see that the right thing was done, and done at once, the government with its supporters saw to it that it was not done, they saw to it that action was held up. The government, through its chief officer, is so much interested in seeing that the right thing is done that it does not know to-day who is being prosecuted, who is being convicted, or whether anybody has been convicted at all. That is where the matter rests. In answer to my question the Minister of Justice says, "I do not know who was convicted". I asked him explicitly whether anybody was convicted, and if so whether that person was still confined or had been let out; but he does not know. Why, the government knows less about the matter than any man on the street knows, because everyone is aware that Baldy Robb was sent out with the government's blessing.
1806	COMMONS
Athabaska Election-Sir George Perley
An bon. MEMBER:	That was another
matter.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: It is the same election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to know all about Baldy Robb. Does he think that Baldy Robb was connected with this particular election?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: No, but it is of the same stripe.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: It is another election.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: It is the same general election, absolutely. Now is there no duty on the part of the government to see that the laws of this Dominion are carried out?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend
leaves Baldy Robb I would suggest, if he wants to know the reason, that he had better inquire of his own leader.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: That is a suggestion the hon. gentleman can safely make in the absence of my hon. leader.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I give you warning.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I have no doubt my leader will look after himself very well if my hon. friend puts the question to him. But is there no responsibility on the government to see to it that the laws, not of the provinces but of the Dominion, are respected? I submit there is. The Minister of Justice says that no counsel was retained by the Dominion in this prosecution; he declares it was not asked for. But the statute does not imply that he should wait to be asked. Section 32 reads:
The Attorney General of Canada shall instruct counsel to assist in any prosecution which is thereon instituted by the local authorities charged with the administration of justice.
The Attorney General was not to wait until he was asked; he was then and there to instruct counsel. Why? Simply to ensure that a proper procedure Should be followed and that the matter should be properly pressed. It was his duty to see to it that the laws of parliament were observed. It is idle to say that the government have done all that they could or ought to do in connection with this whole question. If they say they have then they admit that they are indeed impotent to do anything that should be done to punish election frauds. I got up merely for the purpose of pointing this out. My hon. friends were under an obligation to take steps to see

that misdemeanour was punished, and not to throw the whole responsibility on the local authorities. Section 32 of our own act declares that counsel must be appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: When there are proceedings.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
But my hon.
friend does not know whether there were any proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Has my hon. friend read the report?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I have just
quoted the section. It is a question for my hon. friend to ascertain whether there were proceedings or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: My hon. friend does not know about any proceedings having been taken, and he appointed no counsel. If he is content to leave it there, I am.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I
regret exceedingly that my leader is not here to-day. This is a question which he has studied closely and he is much interested to see that justice is done and that parliament shall do something to remedy the iniquities of the election in question. It is all very well for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), to say that this is a matter for parliament. Of course it is a matter for parliament. But hon. gentlemen opposite have a very nice way of shedding their responsibility on to parliament when they want to, and at other times doing things and then bringing them to parliament for ratification afterwards. Who are in the majority on the committee on privileges and elections?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
We are blamed if we
do and we are blamed if we don't.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
The government have a majority on this committee. The Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) are both members of the committee and therefore, by reason of their position in this house, they have a greater responsibility in relation to the work of the committee on privileges and elections than any other single member could have. I submit, therefore, that it is a most extraordinary thing that in a matter of this sort the privileges and elections committee could not get a meeting together last year, and it seems to me that the responsibility rests on the government, with a majority in the house, to see that there shall be a meeting of the committee to consider the question.

Athabaska Election-Mr. Kellner
I want to say a few words regarding another matter which is associated with this question. One of the candidates in the election, Mr. Geauvreau, was not returned his deposit. According to the figures given by the returning officer he did not receive half as many votes as the man who was elected, but I submit that this is a case where some consideration ought to be given to this man by reason of the extraordinary circumstances of the election. Who knows how many votes were cast in the election? I say, no one knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Was he a third candidate?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Yes, he was a
third candidate. But I say no one knows how many votes were cast at the election. I want to read a few extracts from the report of Mr. Justice Clarke, and I could read many others of a similar kind. I took the statement with reference to Cold Lake poll No. 212a, at page 2 of the report:
The list contains 402 names, which is more than double the number of persons qualified to vote.
Then poll No. 212(a) (2), another section of the foregoing poll:
^ The poll book and statement of the poll show 73 to have voted, as follows: 54 for Cross, 3 for Geauvreau 16 for Kellner. I find that approximately 27 of the persons named in the poll book as having voted did not vote, and most of them are unknown.
At page 3 of the report, in connection with Reita Lake poll No. 220, there appears the following:
I find that what purports to be the voter's list for this poll and to be signed by Thomas J. Cardinal as registrar, and returned with the election papers contains 73 names, and that not more than ten persons were entitled to vote in this division: that no such person as Thomas J. Cardinal is known in the neighbourhood.
And further down on the same page:
I find that the poll book is a forgery as no votes were polled and no poll was held.
Under these circumstances it is rather unfair that any one of the candidates in that election should lose his deposit. I understand that Mr. Geauvreau has made a claim to the Auditor General for the return of his deposit. On the face of the return, in accordance with the law, the Auditor General could not very well return him his deposit, but I submit to the government that this is a matter which they might very well consider from another point of view altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: How many votes did he poll ?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: We do not know. Who knows? Do you know? I submit that is a very unfair question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I mean, on the return as it is.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: The Minister of Justice is well aware that no one knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I mean, on the return as made.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: He polled only 643, according to the return. From the evidence given before Mr. Justice Clarke is that any proof as to how many votes he polled? I submit there is no proof whatever, and I suggest to the Minister of Justice that he consider this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I admit that is a fair argument for my hon. friend to make.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I think in all fairness, under these circumstances, something should be done. I do not think the Auditor General can do it, but I think this parliament and this government Should see that an amount is placed in the estimates to provide for the return of his deposit to this man, because there was really no election actually held in that constituency.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak I wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Sir George Perley). I also agree that no one could tell in any way how many votes were polled in this election, and I might also point out that if it were so very easy to poll votes which did not exist it might be equally easy to destroj' some of the legitimate votes which were polled. While my opponent in that election, Mr. Geauvreau, only polled some 645 votes, it is quite reasonable to suppose that some of the other votes might have been polled close to a river, and that the ballot box containing perhaps some further votes for him disappeared therein. Therefore I think in all fairness that his application for the return of his deposit should be considered.
I want to join with some of the statements which have been made in regard to an investigation by the committee to see if something cannot be done in connection with the plugging of lists, the holding of polls in districts where no one lives and the return of supposed votes in districts and in polls where no votes were cast, and beyond that I wish to introduce a few other matters which none of the previous speakers has brought

Athabaska Election-Mr. Kellner
up for consideration. In the first place, if you refer to section 50, sub-section 4, of the Dominion Elections Act, you will see that it provides that the printer shall file an affidavit giving the number of ballot papers printed, and also containing the statement that no other ballot papers were printed. In this particular election an affidavit was filed by the printer giving the number of ballots printed, but a peculiar thing which happened in that election was that there were two sets of ballots. On some of the ballots my own name was incorrectly spelled, as was the name of the Conservative candidate, while on the remainder of the ballots our names were spelled correctly. No reference to that was made in the affidavit. I think it reasonable to say that if you can make a slight error in the spelling of a candidate's name there is no limit to the distance you can go in that direction. For instance, if during an election it is presumed to be correct to mis-spell the name of a candidate, why could you not transpose all the letters of his name so that no one would know who was meant? As an example, supposing you transposed the first and last letters of the name of the Prime Minister.
We must also recall that the printer is required to make an affidavit stating the number of ballots printed, the amount of paper used and the disposition which was made of the balance of the paper. If some 15,000 or 20,000 ballots were printed on which the names were incorrectly spelled; if these ballots were. sent out for general use in the election and were not included in the affidavit, how could an affidavit be made giving the amount of the paper used and the disposition made of the balance?
Then I pass from that question to the requirement that the returning officer stamp the ballots. That section of the act is very clear and very drastic; it provides that the returning officer must stamp each and every ballot used, and that anyone not being a returning officer, having) in his possession any stamp, imitation or counterfeit, is guilty of an indictable offence. In this particular case, as was stated by a previous speaker, the returning officer lived in Lac la Biche, while the ballots were stamped by a man in Edmonton; they were never sent to Lac la Biche, and the returning officer did not even know who printed them. Is that in conformity with the requirements of the act, =r is that something for a committee of this aouse to deal with?
Provision is also made with regard to the distribution of the ballot. In this particular case it was shown that the ballots were sent
IMr. Kellner.]
out by automobile, by mail and I presume by every other conceivable method which could be made use of. For instance, we are prepared to prove, if it has not been done already and I am not sure whether it came up in the investigation, that two or three men in automobiles w'ent from poll to poll asking the returning officer if he had all the ballots he required, and if he had not they gave him some. I am sure the Minister of Justice is reasonably familiar with the provisions of the act, and I wonder if he thinks that is carrying out the provisions of that act or whether it is an additional reason fot referring this question to the committee, with the understanding that these various sections will be definitely decided upon, so that in the future we may have some sort of ruling or authority to follow? I just wish to read a part of what Judge Clarke says with regard to that particular matter, which will be found at page 8 of his report:
The office of the returning officer was at Lac la Biche and the ballots were printed in Edmonton, more than one hundred miles distant. Instead of coming to Edmonton with the stamp or haring the ballots sent to Lac la Biche to be stamped before they were bound up in pads suitable for delivery the stamp was sent to William R. Wilson of Edmonton, for the purpose of having him stamp the ballots on behalf of the returning officer, which he did, and then returned the stamp to the returning officer. There is nothing to indicate any wrong doing in connection with the printing, stamping or distribution of the ballots except that the stamping was done by Wilson and not by the returning officer.
Section 51 (f) of the act makes it an offence punishable with severe penalties for anyone not being a returning officer to have the stamp in his possession, and I am asked to find Wilson guilty of that offence. With some doubt I have come to the conclusion that I should not do so. It is true that Wilson did, in a sense, have possession of the stamp, but he held it for the returning officer, in whose possession I think it could he fairly said to be. and having regard to the different senses in which the word "possession" is used, and the severe penalties attached to the offence I think it is not the intention of the act that such possession as Wilson had was an offence.
I presume that if another case is brought up under this act this judgment by Mr. Justice Clarke will be cited as a precedent, and this is what it amounts to: Supposing in the Peace River country you had a returning officer living up in the Pouce Coupe country. He could send that stamp down to Baldy Robb and say, "You stamp all the ballots you require and send them out as you please." Or the returning officer might live up in the Athabaska constituency say at Lac la Biche; he could send the stamp down to that mutual friend of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and myself, Mr. Bowtell, and say,

Athabaska Election-Mr. Kellner
" Harry, you stamp them and send them out." As far as I can see there is no way of keeping any track of the number of ballots sent out or where they are sent, and I am sure the election act never anticipated anything of that kind.
I might refer to another clause in the act which provides that in the event of any civil servant, or anyone else for that matter, being proven guilty, or pleading guilty to an offence under this act, in addition to other penalties, he shall not be permitted to hold any office within the nomination of the crown. When that was mentioned a minute ago the Minister of the Interior stated that some fifteen government officials had been discharged following the discussion of this matter in the house last year. I am afraid that he would have a hard time trying to find that number of officials that had been discharged. I believe the sendees of one were dispensed with; I believe the Minister of the Interior did discharge the land agent at Lac la Biche. Outside of that I do not think there were any. I am pretty sure I would know it if what the Minister of the Interior states is correct. I repeat, there was but a single civil servant discharged in the constituency.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend who were the government employees who were before Judge Clarke or who were in any way implicated? I am really interested in getting this information because any of those in my department who were proved guilty are certainly not in the employ of the department to-day.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I could not give the minister that information offhand. I do not think it would be a difficult matter to find out, and if I were getting the information I should have to have assistance of the department. However, I am quite sure there is quite a number of them.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: It is hardly fair for my hon. friend to make assertions of that kind unless he is prepared to back them up with evidence. In acting as I did I acted according bo the evidence taken by Mr. Justice Clarke. If there are any guilty parties in my department-and I do not know of any-they will be dismissed forthwith.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I can give the names of some and what disposition was made of theil cases, and will do so in a moment. First of all I should like to offer a few comments on the assertions which various ministers made last year, to the effect that they were in favour of cleaning up this matter. If we are to take the statements of the ministers, they are
very much in favour of getting rid of those civil servants who were guilty of the offences in question, and I suppose they will go further and say that they are not in favour of employing any of the others who were implicated. The Minister of the Interior said that the postmaster at Lac la Biche had been discharged. Now I want to deal in some detail with t'he post office at that place, and show what took place there. I am glad that the Postmaster General (Mr. Yeniot) is here because he will be able to correct me if I err in any statement I may make. The postmaster at Lac la Biche was not discharged. There was, however, a case against him of having incited one of the witnesses in the investigation to perjury, and we felt quite sure that we could convict him on that charge. I was probably a little indiscreet because at a meeting I said that if he were left in the office I was going to see whether we could not persuade the government to proceed against him on the charge referred to. Almost immediately he resigned. I do not know whether his resignation was because of that statement or whether it was merely a coincidence. Anyway he resigned.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: That was at Lac la Biche?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Yes, Lac la Biche.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
That postmaster resigned
on request after investigation was made.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I was citing the information which I think I obtained from the Civil Service Commission. If he was fired, so much the better.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission had nothing whatever to do with his resignation.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
The Postmaster General
is evidently trying to get me to say something I have no intention of saying. I did not say they had anything to do with the investigation. I said the Civil Service Commission advertised the position and they did. There were three applicants. One was ruled out as ineligible because he did not reside within the district. That cut the number down to two. One of these was Clovis Hamel, son of the former postmaster, P. D. Hamel. The other was a man by the name of J. L. Lavoie. The latter had been a bank teller for three or four years, and had considerable business experience. At the time the Civil Service Commission had the position under review, I submitted the evidence which had been given in the case of the Lac la Biche polls. That covered both polls. Clovis Hamel, who was making application for the position

Athabaska Election-Mr. Kellner
of postmaster, was the deputy returning officer in one poll. When we started to investigate the happenings at the Lac la Biche polls we hoped to prove that a large number of voters, after voting in one poll, had gone over and polled their votes at the other booth. Unfortunately when we got the election returns the poll book for one of the Lac la Biche polls was missing. Now the responsibility for destroying that book was sought to be placed on Isaac Gagnon who had been returning officer, the man whose name has already been mentioned here as being unable to read or write. I consider the attempt to fasten this charge on the late Mr. Gagnon was the most despicable thing I have ever seen in my life. I do not for a moment believe that Mr. Gagnon destroyed that poll book; I think that some persons who are now occupying positions under the government destroyed it. However, that is only my personal opinion. Mr. Lavoie made application for this position, and after the Civil Service Commission had given due consideration to the application, he was appointed. A little later on the Post Office Department refused to accept the appointment, and then there was only one applicant left, namely, Clovis Hamel, the son of P. D. Hamel who had been fired. The result was that Clovis Hamel was made postmaster. Clovis also got the appointment of land agent, and P. D. was never relieved of his position as telegraph operator. So here is what the government accomplished in that case: They took the post office and the land office away from the father and gave them to the son. As regards the position of telegraph operator, P. D. Hamel had the position before and he still holds it.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
