speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: That is what I want to get from my hon. friend. You do not say that?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I will make it very plain to the minister. Here is what took place: We submitted-perhaps I had better say I submitted-the evidence to the Civil Service Commission covering the investigation, but we could not prove what we started out to strove owing to one poll book at Lac la Biche saving disappeared. In the case of the other poll we did prove that they had taken ballots for quite a number of persons, sixteen or eighteen people, that never voted. In the poll, where Clovis Hamel was deputy returning officer, we did prove that one man, who
Air- Kellner.]
was in the town of Waterways on election day, was recorded as having voted. Of course he could not have voted in Lac la Biche when he was in Waterways. The minister will know that well enough. Another man who operates a store-he is a Serbian, I think, and I am satisfied is not a citizen of Canada-voted although his name was not on the voters' list. He was not challenged and did not have someone to verify his identity as the act requires. There were two charges against Clovis Hamel wihch the evidence will prove at any time. Now Judge Clarke makes no comment on them in the report. I think the minister will admit that where there were such offences, an infraction of the law covering merely two or three votes would be hardly worth mentioning.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: That is just what I want to bring out. My hon. friend has mentioned what I have contended all the time, that not a word was said about it in Judge Clarke's report. My statement is now, and has been all the time, that every one of the cases mentioned in Judge Clarke's report has been dealt with. And may I say further: If my hon. friend will prove his contention when this investigation goes on- as I hope it will; no one hopes it more than I do-every one of the people who have been found guilty of offences will be punished. I want to say this with reference to my hon. friend-

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: All right. I will make a statement later.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
The Speaker will give
me extra time for this interruption. I was just thinking that the Minister of the Interior should have directed his remarks to the Minister of Public Works in regard to Mr. P. D. Hamel, in connection with his occupying the position of telegraph operator there. He is not arguing that he was discharged from that position.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I am speaking of my own department.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
That, however, is what
took place. You have the post office, the sub-land agency and the telegraph office in the same building they were always in, and you have the same officers operating them with the exception that now the father is working for the son instead of the son working for the father.
I will pass from that to the case of the Heinsburg post office and I want to read a little extract in connection with that from

Athabaska Election-Mr. Kellner
Mr. Justice Clarke's report. On page 6 of the report Mr. Justice Clarke has this to say:
I find that the said William Robertson and W. L. Crook by reason of each aiding in the commission of the offence and each having an intention in common with the other to prosecute an unlawful purpose are both guilty of forging 66 ballots and the poll book.
Let us remember that the poll clerk in that poll is W. L. Crook. He was an official at the poll known as Parenteau during that election. Tributary to his home is a post office known as the Heinsburg post office of which a Mr. L. Coombe was the postmaster. He was a returned man who had spent about four years in the war and had been discharged. This is a small post office and the income is very little, but it was certainly a position valued by that man. He had been running the office for several years and last summer he was notified that the office was to be taken from him and that the new appointee would be Mrs. W. L. Crook, wife of this poll clerk. The matter was brought to my attention along with a petition signed, I am told, by every patron of that office with the exception of the Crook family, requesting that Coombe be retained as postmaster. Here you have the position. Every single patron of the post office, with the exception of W. L. Crook and his family, were satisfied with the man who was in charge of it. I thought this was something that must have been put over without the knowledge of the government so I wrote to the Postmaster General giving him all the details. The Postmaster General wrote me back saying: Yes, Mrs. Crook is the wife of W. L. Crook; but do you think that is any reason why she should be disqualified from taking this office? That is the answer of the Postmaster General. I thought surely the government are not all of that opinion, so I wrote to the Prime Minister and told him about the matter. The Prime Minister replied saying: Yes, I have investigated this case, but the petition was largely a protest against the office being moved. Regardless of whether it was a protest against the office being moved or whether she is qualified or not, is the government going to excuse things like that by giving a postmastership to the wife of a man to whom they cannot give it, and taking it away from a returned soldier, a man who has gone out and defended this country, in order to give it to a woman by the name of Crook and, I presume, crooked by nature, if we are to judge from the evidence we have before us? That is the whole question.
I pass from that to Frog Lake poll. The Minister of the Interior said a minute ago that Harry Bowtell was not in the country at the moment. If he is not, that is news to me, because I am sure he was a short time ago.	He may have left the country now,
but if so his wife is still running the post office. Harry Bowtell has the honour of being mentioned in this report just a little more frequently than anyone else who is mentioned in it. I will read a few of the comments that Mr. Justice Clarke makes. On page 3 of the report I find this:
I find that the said Martin Grasdal, Harry Bowtell, Ernest Yasey and Peter Peterson are guilty of a conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in respect of the matters aforesaid.
Turning over to the next page I find this:
Harry Bowtell is guilty of abetting in the commission of the said offences in violation of section 51.
On the next page we have this:
The deputy returning officer, Peter Peterson, says that he was also registrar for this polling division, and got a voters' list with the ballot box on the morning of election day from Harry Bowtell, which he signed as registrar. The poll book indicates that there were 194 names on tile voters' list, but there appear to have been only four qualified voters in the polling division.
A little further on the commissioner says:
In fact no poll was held and no person voted; the ballots were marked and put in the box by the said Peter Peterson at the instance of the said Harry Bowtell.
Turning over to another page I find that he again speaks of Harry Bowtell in these words:
-and that Harry Bowtell was guilty of abetting in the commission of such offences by reason whereof both of them became disqualified from voting at any election of a member to serve in the House of Commons for a term of seven years.
There are two other references to him, but I want to present the one in connection with Mrs. Bowtell. I find this on page 13 of the report:
In connection with this poll, a cheque was issued by the Auditor General to Thomas J. Cardinal for $24.26 for his services as registrar. No such person existed. The cheque was obtained by Emma A. Bowtell, wife of Harry Bowtell, the postmaster at Frog Lake, and she endorsed on it the name of Thomas J. Cardinal and obtained payment and appropriated the proceeds to her own use, and I find her guilty of forgery in respect thereof.
I should like to stop there long enough to ask the Minister of Justice if that is one of the cases the provincial government would have to prosecute?

Athabaska Election-Mr. Kellner

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: He was given a certificate of indemnity by the judge. Nothing could be done against him.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
That remark from the
Minister of Justice is not in keeping with the high position he occupies. How could a judge give anyone a certificate to preclude a prosecution against that person for forgery? It cannot be done.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend's question was misunderstood by the Minister of Justice. He was answering in regard to Mr. Harry Bowtell. The hon. member was asking a question about Mrs. Bowtell.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: The minister made a remark a little earlier in the afternoon that these prosecutions should be carried on by the provincial government and in his remarks I thought I detected a little complaint, or possibly something stronger, that the provincial government had not taken any action. My suggestion is this: Whose responsibility is it to prosecute in connection with this offence? Surely the Minister of Justice will not say that the provincial government should prosecute in connection with such an offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: My hon. friend is altogether wrong. The matter is one for the provincial authorities.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Let me quote further.
Speaking of the Cushing poll the Commissioner says:
In connection with this poll, a cheque was issued by the Auditor General to P. A. Patterson, for $40, for his services as registrar. No such person existed. The cheque was obtained by Emma A. Bowtell, already mentioned, and by her direction the name of P. A. Patterson was endorsed upon the cheque by her thirteen year old daughter, by means of which Emma A. Bowtell obtained payment and appropriated the proceeds to her own use, and I find her guilty of forgery in respect thereof.
She is the postmistress of the Frog Lake post office, or Harry Bowtell is the postmaster, and she is the postmistress-I do not know which.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I have looked up the post office guide, and I find that Harry Bowtell is still the postmaster of Frog Lake.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
It is in the family anyway. They also have the telegraph office at that point. I am sure the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) will be glad to know that there are still a few of these people in the employ of the government. Summing up these three cases, in Lac la Biche, the son gets the post office, and other appointments. The post office stays in the same building,

it is kept by the same bunch of officials, and I am satisfied that no one could go in there to-day and detect one particle of difference from what it was before. In the case of the Heinsburg post office, you discharged a returned man who had fought for this country for several years during the war, a disabled veteran who required this little bit of support, and you give the post office to the wife of one of these ginks who was convicted. Then in the case of Frog Lake, you had both the wife and the husband. The children were not old enough, but the eldest was also convicted, and you leave them plumb alone. That is what you do, and nothing more.
Let me go a little further. I think anyone will realize that in order to submit the volume of evidence which we did submit in this investigation, it was going to cost us, and did cost us, a considerable amount of money, so I think any fair-minded person will give us credit for not being remiss in our duty if we neglected to bring in a few who should have been brought in or whose names might have been linked up with these others. I think it is fair to say that in a good many of these cases there is a preponderance of evidence, whether it was submitted before a judge or not, that should be taken into consideration. What I would like to ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), is this: Does he think that Charlie Cross's campaign manager could go through that election without being a party to what took place? And he is appointed a land agent at Bonny-ville.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Who was
his election agent? I thought it was Mr. Deyl.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Joe Deschene was his
campaign manager.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is taking some chances in laying an accusation against Mr. Deschene.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I have made a statement that in cases where there is a preponderance of evidence that should be considered. How could anyone be closely associated with that campaign and not know something about what was going on? Regardless of whether I am .taking a chance or not, that is what took place.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will not suggest that all the men in Athabaska who were associated with Mr. Cross-I hold no brief for Mr. Cross, as my hon. friend well knows-would be guilty of wrongdoing.
181:

Alhabaska Election-Mr. Kellner

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
No, I am not making
any such suggestion as that at all, and I do not for the life of me see how the minister can imagine that I am. I am trying to be fair in this, and I am arguing that anybody who was actively associated with that election, either as a candidate, or as taking part in the organization of the machine that put this deal over, could hardly be considered as knowing nothing about what was going on.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I am always loath to believe wrong of anyone until it is proven. I have known Mr. Deschene for a considerable number of years, and I have yet to know of him doing anything wrong.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I would not make any
suggestion about anyone that I did not think was merited, but I cannot for the life of me conceive of any person going through that campaign as manager for the candidate and know nothing about what was going on.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Is my hon. friend correct in saying that Mr. Deschene was the campaign manager? We all know that he was in that election and that he spoke in the election, but this is the first intimation that I have had that he was campaign manager.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I will put it this way.
If the Minister of the Interior has good reasons for thinking he was not, possibly he will submit his reasons to the house, and we will decide the matter.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
That is all
very fine, but my hon. friend is making an accusation, and I am not going to be put in that position.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I do not really know what you are going to do about it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend can do what he likes about it. If he has an accusation to make against Mr. Deschene, let him make it.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
He is making it on his
authority as a sitting member of this house.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
My accusation, if that
is what you choose to call it, has been repeated two or three times already, and there can be no doubt as to the statement I made, and outside of the Minister of the Interior, I venture to say that no one in this house will call my statement an unfair one. Seeing that our friends over there are getting so "het up" over this matter, I think I will just give them a few.
This Liberal party which we have in Canada has sunk, so far as Alberta is concerned, to possibly as low a level as any political party could sink. I have here one of the booklets which were sent all through my constituency, and I expect all over Canada, called, "Hints on Organization and Work on Polling Day". This is sent out by the National Liberal Committee, 115 Sparks street, Ottawa. I want to quote some of the instructions it gives. At page twelve, it says:
If a friendly voter spoils his ballot, see that he gets a new one, and that the spoiled one is marked and cancelled.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: What is wrong with that? He is entitled to a ballot.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Is it fair to ask what
would happen to the unfriendly voter? I quote again:
Once a voter gets a ballot he has a right to use it, 'whether he has been sworn or not. When a friendly voter therefore gets a ballot, he should at once mark it and have it deposited into the box.
In case somebody heads him off, I suppose. It continues:
He cannot be sworn after he gets the ballot paper. Remember this, each ballot is counted, no matter by whom cast.
I ask the Solicitor General, what is the matter with that?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
That is absolutely fair.
There is nothing wrong about that.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: What about the suggestion contained in it?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
There is no suggestion
contained in it. That is perfectly all right.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
If these things appear
to be all right to the members of this government, then certainly it is beyond my powers to point out anything that they would consider irregular, but in spite of that, I am going to give one more quotation:
Only two agents for each candidate are entitled to be present. If possible, arrange to have all objected ballots laid aside before you argue for their rejection or validity, so that you may see how the ballots will affect the count. Examine carefully back and front, each ballot marked for an opposite candidate.
What is the inference there? Is it not this? You take the unfriendly ballots and you put them over here; you take the friendly ballots and you put them over here. Then you size up the two piles, and if the friendly ballots make the biggest pile, argue for the inclusion of the whole thing, but if the un-friendy ballots make the biggest pile, then argue that they should all be rejected. There can be no other interpretation.

Athabaska Election-Mr. Manion
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me address these serious words to the government. Out through that district a very large percentage of the young people are just developing into womanhood and manhood. When I was there last summer the only topic universally discussed was the fact that those who had been proved guilty of illegal practices in the Athabasca election were appointed to these positions. It seems to me that this is what the government is doing. You are saying to the young people of that country: If you go out and forge cheques to help out your party on election day, to put this stuff over, you are all right, you can get a government job; you oan forge cheques, you can beat the Dominion of Canada out of money which you should not have, and nobody will say a word to you; but, on the other hand, if you do not do anything like that, even though you helped your country to fight its wars, your post office will be taken away from you and you will get no consideration at all. Now, sir, is that the impression this government wants (to make on the people in that constituency?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, but a few minutes ago when the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was speaking, the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) interjected a couple of remarks which to my mind, if they are to 'be permitted to go out to this country unchallenged, cast a more or less shameful reflection upon my hon. leader (Mr. Bennett), and I intend to ask the Solicitor General to explain them. The incident occurred when the member for West York was speaking to the effect that Baldy Rob'b had been sentenced to imprisonment for crooked election practices and had been shown clemency. The Solicitor General interjected these words-I took them down at the time and have since had them typed:
t>
-V,r- Sa"Tm' before my hon. friend leaves Baldy Robb, I would say that if he wants to know the reason he had better inquire of his own leader.
Then .the member for West York replied to the effect that his leader could look after himself, and the Solicitor General retorted:
I give you warning.
Now, sir, only one possible conclusion can be drawn from those remarks of the Solicitor General, and as my hon. leader is sick in bed I feel that this shameful implication should be retracted or explained. Either the

Solicitor General has said too much or he has said too little. In justice to my hon. leader I wish to ask the Solicitor General to explain u'hat he referred to in those interjections.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend, I regret as much as he does the absence of the leader of the Conservative party when my friend from West York was addressing the house. If my hon. friend for West Calgary, the leader of the Conservative party, had been present I am quite sure that no reference would have been made to the case of Baldy Robb, for two obvious reasons. First, because the case of Baldy Robb has absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with the present motion. Baldy Robb was connected with the election in the constituency of Peace River, and was in no way connected with the election in the constituency of Athabaska. It goes to show that my hon. friend from West York when addressing the house should have taken more time to examine the motion, its object and its meaning. The second reason why no reference would have been made to the case of Baldy Robb is that that case was dealt with in such a manner and under such circumstances as are well known to the leader of the opposition, and he would have been the first to keep the hon. gentleman from mentioning it in the house.
As to my intention in interjecting what I did interject, I may say that I did not want to cast any shameful reflection on the character of the leader of the Conservative party. I had no such intention. Members of this house know me sufficiently well to be assured that I would have waited for the leader of the Conservative party to be present if I wanted to attack him. I have never had the habit of attacking people in their absence, but on account of the very peculiar circumstances of the case referred to by the member for West York, I thought it was just as well that I should say enough for the incident to close immediately, as it did close, and I may assure-

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: You have not said enough yet.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: -and I assure my hon. friend from Fort William that I attach no shameful interpretation in any way to the conduct of the leader of the opposition in that matter; but if he will discuss it with his own leader he will reach the same conclusion as I have, that we should not discuss it in the house.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
Tell us.

Atliabaska Election-Mr. Manion

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
My hon. friend from St.
Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) wishes to know the reason. Suffice it to say that in all cases of remission of sentence the crown exercises the royal prerogative.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: That exercise of the royal prerogative is not to be debated.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Therefore when the royal prerogative was exercised in the case of Baldy Robb it was exercised for reasons that I cannot discuss here.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Quite so; but why not explain?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: When the member for West York introduced the matter he was placing me in a position as the minister who advised in the matter of being-I would not say accused, but of being suspected of having taken a decision which I should not have taken, when as a matter of fact I acted after consulting many people and inquiring in many quarters. I cannot say any further, but in fairness to the minister in charge-

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Why did you give the warning?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: In view of the special prerogative which is exercised in such matters, in view of the parliamentary practice in similar cases, and in view of the fact that the motion before the house is in no way connected with the case of Baldy Robb, I think that incident should not have been introduced here at all.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: If the Solicitor General will allow a question-in reference to the explanations which have been made, and which are highly honourable to the hon. gentleman, does he still make any aspersions on the leader of the opposition?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I never made any. I
want to make that very plain-I never made any.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: What was the warning for?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: The warning that I gave to my hon. friend from West York was that he should not discuss that matter at all because apparently he was not familiar with it, and I am quite sure he was not.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Cheap.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
My hon. friend may
consider it cheap, but I think that what I said was said in fairness to everyone. I have no intention of casting aspersions on the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and if my hon. friends opposite think so they are entirely under a false impression.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I am glad you say that.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: If I wanted to attack the leader of the opposition I certainly would not do so when he was away. I never attack any man in his absence.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
answered the question to his own satisfaction, but when he says that he meant to make no attack on the leader of the opposition, I wish to say that he thinks too late, because he made the attack in these very statements. And immediately upon hearing these statements from the hon. gentleman I said to myself, "Either Mr. Bennett has done something shameful or the Solicitor General has no right to make any such statements."

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Has my hon. friend concluded his remarks?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: No; I am going to conclude them now.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Well, what was I doing?

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
You were answering my
question.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
In that case I will allow
my hon. friend to conclude his remarks and then I will speak.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
I will conclude very quickly. The point I am making is this: that had I not asked the Solicitor General the question I did, there would without a doubt have gone out to the whole country through the press, and rightly, the suggestion from the Solicitor General that the hon. member for West Calgary, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), had done something shameful or disgraceful in connection with the clemency shown Baldy Robb. This certainly was the only possible inference that anyone could have drawn from the Solicitor General's remarks -that if the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) did not bring to a close his observations in reference to the clemency shown Baldy Robb, he, the Solicitor General, wanted to warn him that he was going to show up the leader of the opposition. That is the only possible sense which could be read into the statement of the Solicitor General. What other conclusion could one draw from it? The hon. member for West York had

At.habaska Election-Mr. Cannon
been speaking of the clemency shown Baldy Robb, and he made some remark to the effect that the government had been very kind to him, or something of that sort. I do not remember the exact words. The Solicitor General then interjects the remark: "Before my hon. friend leaves Baldy Robb I would suggest, if he wants to know the reason, that he had better inquire of his own leader."

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
No royal
prerogative against insinuation.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: And later on the Solicitor General adds: "I give you warning." In other words-and this is the only inference-he wa3 giving warning to the hon. member for West York that if he persisted in his remarks regarding Baldy Robb he, the Solicitor General, would show up the leader of the opposition as having been in some shameful way connected with Baldy Robb. I accept completely the Solicitor General's withdrawal but I certainly find it difficult to understand his explanation.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I wish to say first of all that I do not withdraw anything I said.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: My hon. friend withdrew his implication; he did so three or four times -the implication of guilt.

If any information, indictment or penal action is at any time after an inquiry pending in any court against such witness in respect of any corrupt or illegal practices committed by him previously to the time of his giving his evidence, at any election concerning which he has been so examined, the court shall, on production and proof of such certificate, stay such proceedings, and may, in its discretion, award to him any costs to which he has been put.

Again I repeat that this matter must be discussed in the light of the law as it exists, not in the light of wbat my hon. friend, or any other gentleman opposite, would like it to be. speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: I think the house is very glad indeed that the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), if he did not withdraw the implication contained in his remark, as we understood it, at least assures us that he had not intended any such implication. Certainly when I heard him I felt he was making some reflection on the (honour of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and I am glad to know that is not the case. Among other points raised by the hon. member for Athabaska, he called attention to-

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
permit me, in order that we may argue the case with the facts before us. The Minister of Justice informs me1 that Mirs. Bowtell was granted a certificate of immunity.

subtopic: REPORTS OF HON. MR. JUSTICE CLARKE
speechtext: Not for forgery.

With respect to those found guilty of illegal and corrupt practices under the Elections Act the commissioner could grant a certificate of indemnity, but the hon. member for Athabaska has pointed out that in addition to those there was the case of Mrs. Bowtell who forged the endorsements on cheques issued by the government and received and applied the proceeds to her own use. Now I say to the hon. gentleman that in the case of the forgery of a Dominion cheque and the defalcation of Dominion funds the Department of Justice has, from time immemorial, undertaken the prosecution of its own officials who have forged such cheques and forged such endorsements. I know of at least ten or fifteen cases in the last thirty years where such prosecutions have been undertaken by the Department of Justice. That is the point which my hon. friend the Solicitor General is entirely avoiding. Now supposing the commissioner did hold an inquiry in connection with corrupt practices and did give a certificate of indemnity to Mrs. Bowtell. That indemnity would be no defence to the prosecution of Mrs. Bowtell for the forgery of Dominion cheques and the misappropriation of Dominion funds. I think there is no doubt about that. However, I am not going to stress the point further; I simply give that as mjr clear opinion.
Now chapter 51 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, provides that the commissioners shall report with respect to each election the names of all persons whom they find to have been guilty of corrupt or illegal practices therein. May I point out that "corrupt or illegal practices" has a special definition, and I do not think that the forgery of Dominion cheques and wrongful appropriation of Dominion funds comes within it. The commissioners are required to report the names. To whom are they required to report? Section 28 says that the commissioners shall from time to time report to the Governor General the evidence taken and what they find concerning the premises. The report is made to the Governor General, in reality to the government of the country, in order that such action as may be deemed necessary in the premises may be taken. The report which is made to parliament is rather a subsidiary matter, because the act proceeds to state in section 30 that every such report which has been made to the Governor General shall be submitted to parliament within fourteen days after such report is made if parliament is sitting, or if parliament is not then sitting, within fourteen days from the next meeting. So not only is the government to receive a report for its iiv-



Athabaska Election-Mr. Cahan
formation, but parliament is also to receive the report for the same reason. The report when it is received by the government shall be laid before the Attorney General of Canada, the Minister of Justice. Now the Minister of Justice has a special duty to perform in the premises. It is his duty to examine the evidence, and if he finds sufficient evidence available for a prosecution he must certify such information to the Secretary of State, who in turn must communicate the report, with the evidence, to the lieutenant governor of the province in which the election was held. But in addition to that, the statute places a duty upon the Attorney General of Canada in respect of his office, and his official duty in the premises is expressed in section 32, which says that:
_ The Attorney General of Canada shall instruct counsel to assist in any prosecution which is thereon instituted by the local authorities charged with the administration of justice.
The word "shall" is used. The Attorney General of Canada "shall" instruct counsel. It is not within his discretion to refrain from making the appointment of counsel. It is a duty incumbent upon him under the statute so to act in this matter, therefore it is his duty to ascertain the result of the transmission of this report to the lieutenant governor of the province. It is his duty to ascertain whether the attorney general or crown prosecutor or other authority in the province has undertaken to prosecute for these offences. He must keep himself informed in regard to these matters. When a prosecution is undertaken, section 32 states that the Attorney General of Canada shall instruct counsel to assist in any prosecution.
I am the last one to endeavour to impose upta the Minister of Justice any duties which dc not properly belong to him. I know he often has to be and has been absent from his office performing very high and onerous duties as representative of Canada in other countries. I do not know whether or not he was absent on this occasion; I do not know who was fulfilling his functions as the acting attorney general during his absence; but I say that under the statutes the Attorney General of Canada, or whoever was acting as Attorney General of Canada, has been utterly negligent and faithless in the performance of his duties in the premises. I say that, because we have had the admission to-day that no counsel was instructed by the Department of the Attorney General of Canada. I am not making any suggestions in regard to the present incumbent; I do not know who was fMr. Cahan.]
acting at the time; but this is a case in which the Attorney General, or the acting Attorney General of Canada for the time being, has not performed his duties under the statute. If he had performed his duties under the statute we would not have had the Solicitor General or the Attorney General, the Minister of Justice, suggesting to-day to the house that they were unaware of the results of the various prosecutions which were undertaker! by the crown prosecutor in the province in question. That is my point, and I think that should have been met more fully than it has been.
Just one other point. I think we all as members of this house must recognize that a duty is placed upon the house and especially upon the government with regard to the reconsideration of the provisions of the Corrupt Practices Act, the Elections Act and the registration of voters thereunder. It is impossible, as will be admitted, for any private member to procure with any facility amendments to the public acts of Canada, especially public acts such as the Corrupt Practices Act, the Elections Act, and all the rest. But certain kinds of illegal acts which were so prevalent in the constituency of Athabaska are prevalent in our city of Montreal to an enormous extent. I drew the attention of the house to this once before when this matter came up. I pointed out that in the electoral district of St. Lawrence-St. George before my first election I found on the list more than two thousand fictitious names. At the last election at which I was a candidate I found more than two thousand fictitious names on the list, and at the present time, although I have not counted them, I am sure that coming in from the provincial registration and otherwise there are already on the list which would form the basis of a new revision, many hundreds of fictitious names. We all know that at elections certain gangs of men are hired in the city and men are even imported from outside to do impersonating. We know there are hundreds of impersonations of registered electors. We know that gentlemen who are late going down town after breakfast find that others have voted in their names.
Why have there been no prosecutions in those cases?

Because no individual alone has the funds or the means to prosecute a thousand people. I am not saying whether this is due to the efforts of the Liberal party or of the Conservative party; but in any

Athabaska Election-Mr. Cahan
of our constituencies in Montreal, in the municipal elections, largely in the provincial elections and still more largely in the federal elections, there are impersonations not by the hundred but by the thousand.
Is it not a fact that these men when caught have been let off with neither fine nor imprisonment? Have they not been dealt with in the most lenient fashion?

I think so, but perhaps I have been so much concerned with the conviction of some of them that I may not be able to give an impartial opinion. You get together an executive committee of the most honourable and honest men you can find in your constituency, men whose reputations are above reproach, men who assist, on election day in the ordinary election work of the constituency, even those who represent you at the poll. Then there are issued in the city of Montreal blanket warrants purporting to be signed by judges; in fact I have seen some myself purporting to be signed by a judge of the court of sessions. I do not know whether they are forgeries or not, but these blanket warrants have been issued by the hundred and put into the hands of police constables for the purpose of arresting early in the morning the most reputable men of the city so as to prevent them from taking part in the election. I am not accusing anybody. The Minister of Justice, I know, is as anxious as I am to put an end to that sort of thing and I believe the other members of the government are equally anxious.
But when the provincial lists in Montreal are prepared, it is impossible for me in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George to ascertain whether proper names are going on the list. Under the provincial law people can register for St. Lawrence-iSt. George at La-chine; they can register ten miles out of my district on the other side of the river; they oan register at Pointe aux Trembles. It would take more than my personal revenue in a year to keep track of the registration of the names of voters in my constituency on the provincial list which go automatically on the Dominion list, so that it is impossible to have any effective supervision of the list until it forms the basis of the Dominion list. In my constituency at the last revision I found more than two thousand fictitious names. That meant that I had to have two thousand individual affidavits made as to whether or not on a certain day those people were residing at the places of residence stated in the 56103-1164
list. That meant that I had to hire men by the hundred to go out and make inquiries at those residences on that day and then make [DOT] individual affidavits. That expense is placed upon me; I have to bear it myself. I am not wealthy; but that expense, which applies also to other city constituencies, is so high that at the present time in the city of Montreal no honest, respectable citizen of moderate means can afford to run a federal election and to pay his own election expenses. Those two thousand affidavits were put in, and what I did was quite fair and frank. I gave a list of the whole two thousand applications to the representative of the gentleman who was opposing me. I do not presume that he knew anything about the matter, but someone knew about it. I said to them: send out to those addresses and if you can find one of them that represents anybody who by chance is not living at that address but is living in any other part of the constituency or anywhere where under the law he has a right to vote, I will not press the objection. After a complete search, I believe there were found out of over two thousand names some fifty residents who had moved from one house in one part of the constituency to another. We sent our agents out, two and two together, to deal with these fifty or sixty residents, and we dealt with them in a satisfactory manner. But the expense of all that, and the expense of revision in my constituency, with over two thousand fictitious names and thousands more coming in at the time of revision, is so great that it costs from four to five thousand dollars at the time of the federal revision simply to supervise this nefarious work and to prevent it having full effect. I know there are members on the other side of the house who complain of exactly the same conditions. When we make prosecutions before the court of sessions, the prosecutions are delayed and delayed and delayed and finally result in nothing. Members cannot initiate one thousand or two thousand prosecutions and then employ a sufficient number of lawyers to appear at the court of sessions day after day, and week after week, and even month after month. It is a scandal that must be prevented in the future. I ask the government, through the Minister of Justice, either through this committee or some other committee, to initiate as a government undertaking, because you need the force and power of will of government to put it through, a reconsideration of our electoral law with a view to making euch amendments in the law governing the revision of
The Royal Assent

the electoral lists in the city of Montreal- and conditions, I have no doubt, ajre the same in other cities-as will give us fair and honest lists that will preclude impersonation and perjury, and enable our committees of honest and representative men to do their electoral work on election day, without being subject to arrest on false and fraudulent warrants and to confinement in the police station under the control of the police until election day is past. It is a scandal. My hon. friend from the west said that conditions out there imperilled responsible democratic government. Democratic government in the city of Montreal in federal elections is at an end, democratic representation is at an end-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Did such a state of
things exist when we were using the provincial lists for federal elections? Is not the condition may hon. friend speaks of the result of that change in the method of making up the lists?

I daresay it is, to a very considerable extent; and remember, I am not charging the Minister of Justice, or the government with Which he is associated, or even the party with which he is associated in the province of Quebec, as being responsible for the iniquities which are perpetrated. I am not charging that, but I say it is a matter in respect of which we ought, on both sides of the house, to come to some reasonable understanding, and we ought to adopt and carry through such measures as may be calculated to put an end to it. To me personally it does not matter. The greatest kindness the Minister of Justice could do to me, as he suggested the other day he should do in the public interest, would be to prevent my representing a Montreal district in this house. But I come in contact with many young men in that city-young men not only of my own race, because my race is in a minority in Montreal, but the best young men who are coming out of the Montreal universities, Liberals as well as Conservatives, and they truthfully say that in view of the conditions " which now exist, it is impossible for young men to attain any eminence in the political life of this country unless they are prepared to become a part of the party machine, on one side or the other, take party funds by thousands and tens of thousands of dollars, and participate in the iniquities which are prevalent, not only one side but on both sides in that city.

Mr. Speaker, I think the time will not be lost that is devoted to a further consideration of
[Mr. Cahan.l
this case. So important is it that I do not think that any matters which are extraneous or are related only indirectly to it should be considered by this house in this connection. The facts are that this election was the most shocking and the most astounding one ever held in the Dominion of Canada, so far as we have any information. The Baldy Robb election in Peace River was held at the same time. It is true that the man who occupied front stage in that election does not come into the inquiry which I am sure will follow this resolution; nevertheless, the fact that the things he did, and kindred things, were repeated in the Athabaska election makes it all the more necessary that we should look to the dignity of this house and our own personal honour, because that is what the question involves.
This report was laid on the table of the house on the 15th day of December, 1926. Who is in control of parliament? The Prime Minister and his cabinet. Who has to deal with a matter of this kind? The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). We come down to this very day and we find that nothing was done or even suggested during the last session of parliament in regard to this report. To-day we find that the Minister of Justice says:	Oh, I am in favour of the resolution.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) says: There will be no one who will be more pleased than I if this resolution carries; and the very words of the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) were, "I have absolutely no objection whatsoever to the motion." Has it come to this, Mr. Speaker, in this parliament, that where the honour of all members is concerned it must devolve upon a private member to bring forward a resolution which will be passed unanimously by the house? There is not a member of this house who will dare to vote against this resolution.

I am sure that other members who have been in the house for the time I have must have been enlivened this afternoon at the unsuccessful attempt of the Solicitor General to extricate himself from the dilemma in which he found himself, due to his unfortunate remark in regard to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The task was too great even for the adroit Solicitor General. It was as transparent as the smoke screen which he undertook to throw around the inaction of the government in dealing with the matters referred to in this house in connection with the resolution of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland).
I was somewhat surprised that hon. members who have advanced information in regard to what happened in the constituency of Athabaska, Peace River, Montreal and other constituencies, should speak as if that were something new in the history of elections in this country. I can remember as far back as twenty-three years ago when the first federal election was held at which a member was elected to this house from the constituency of Yukon. Up in that territory we had a great conglomerate population. No party lines had been drawn. It was the first occasion on which we had been permitted to send a member here. Feeling ran high. The government was popular in some quarters, and unpopular in others. It was never anticipated that violations of the act such as have been described here this afternoon as happening in the Athabaska constituency would appear in the Yukon in those days, and no particular precautions were taken to guard the polls or to safeguard the interest of the opposition. What happened? From a situation which seemed hopeless from the government standpoint, the government candidate was elected with hundreds of a majority to spare. How was it done? By the most unblushing stuffing of ballot boxes. At polls *where there were not thirty people entitled
to vote, ballot boxes were opened showing two hundred ballots marked for the government candidate, and in some of these boxes there was not even to be found a voters' list. The voters' lists were made up of fictitious names to tally with the number of marked ballots found in the boxes after they arrived in the town of Dawson. At one poll where there were not over forty residents entitled to vote a special train was run in from the Alaskan town of Skagway, filled with longshoremen and gamblers, men who had no right to vote in Canada, and they were voted and revoted until hundreds of ballots had been polled for the government candidate. That was our first experience of a Dominion election in the constituency of Yukon in 1902.
Two years went by and the general election of 1904 oame on. Under the Elections Act of that day there was no provision whereby the enumerators who prepared the voters' lists were obliged to give to anyone but the deputy returning officers copies of the lists. So it was impossible for an elector to know until he went into the polling station on election day whether or not his name was on the list of voters. If it was not there he was out of luck; he had to leave without voting. These enumerators were undertaking to exercise their legal right in witholdimg copies of the lists, but having in mind their experience of two years before, the electors were not in a mood to leave anything to chance. So they formed committees and waited on those enumerators. Law or no law, they demanded copies of the lists, and in several instances those enumerators were induced, by proper persuasion, to produce certified copies. What happened then in the case of the great majority of enumerators?

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SITTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I submit the hon. gentleman is not speaking to the motion before the house. Everyone of us on this side could say a lot about What happened in our constituencies on previous elections.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SITTING
speechtext: Go to it.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SITTING
speechtext:
The balance of
those enumerators, in view of what had happened to their fellows, ran for protection to the barracks of the Northwest Mounted Police at Dawson, seeking protection, as they said, from violence. The only violence that was sought to be done to them was to. demand that they should give the opposition copies of the voters' lists. The officer commanding the Northwest Mounted Police, being entirely impartial and desiring only to keep the peace, was in an awkward predica-
1830	COMMONS
Athabaska Election-Mr. Black (Yukon)
ment. A committee consisting of about one hundred citizens of Dawson waited on him. The committee was composed of men of both shades of politics, Liberal and Conservative, and from all walks of life, clergymen, professional men, labourers, artisans and miners. They made it quite clear to the commanding officer that they required copies of these voters' lists the election being only two days away, and they made it manifest to him that they were going to have these copies. I remember very well-

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SITTING
speechtext:
I hope that the hon.
member will bring his argument to bear on the motion before the house. It has reference to the Athabaska election.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SITTING
speechtext:
I hope so, Mr. Speaker. I am stating those occurrences simply to show how necessary it has been, and is now, that the government give serious attention to the amendment and improvement of the Elections Act. I say I remember very well the words of an eminent Presbyterian divine who was a member of the committee that waited on the officer commanding the mounted police. He explained that he was not there threatening violence, that he was a man of peace, but he pointed out how necessary it was that the public should have copies of the voters' lists in view of what had occurred two years before, and he said:
When I came into this country I did as most men, I brought with me a Winchester rifle, and I have it to-day hanging on the wall of my study. I have plenty of ammunition, and if it becomes necessary in order to get these voters' lists, I am prepared to take that rifle off the wall and use it.
The officer asked the committee to withdraw and to return later in lesser numbers. During their absence he communicated with the government candidate and made it known to him that in his opinion the lists should be produced otherwise he could not be responsible for the lives of certain people in that territory. The upshot was that the lists were produced. It was found that hundreds of opposition names had been deliberately struck off and there and then under the eyes of that committee they were put back on the lists.
To show you, sir, how far some people will go in violation of the election law, at that very same election a poll was established at a point on the Pelly river, some four hundred miles away from Dawson. Nobody lived there. It was made a polling division and a poll was supposed to be held there on election day. What was done? In anticipation of electing the government candidate, a deputy returning officer, a poll clerk and a 
messenger were sent off from Dawson City with ballot boxes and a supply of four hundred ballots. They went up the main trail, thence up the Pelly river for a couple of miles, and camped in a tent a few miles from the telegraph station. What were they to do? They were to wait there until election night, then come down to the telegraph station and find out how many ballots were needed to elect the government candidate; then they were to go back to their camp, make up their list, mark the necessary ballots, come into town with them, and the government candidate would be elected. But their plan did not come off. The people had been warned and two days before the election warrants were sworn out for those men charging them with conspiracy under the criminal code, and they were brought into town under arrest before they could mark their fraudulent ballots. In that way ballot box stuffing was prevented and the opposition candidate was elected. What happened then? Hon. members have expressed surprise that persons involved in the election scandal in Athabaska were not punished, but were allowed to remain in government positions. Well, in Yukon the government candidate himself, who was chiefly responsible for the scandals in those two elections, defeated in 1904, was immediately appointed by the then government to a position of responsibility and substantial remuneration as a reward for his services, as were others. Charges were laid against a large number of officials engaged in that election, and no less than fourteen were sent up for tial on charges of conspiracy. What happened to them? On orders from Ottawa the crown prosecutor nolle prosequi'd in each case and dropped the prosecution.
Though the law needs amendment yet, we do not have election scandals in Yukon any more. Why? Not because of the law, but because public opinion precludes their recurrence, and would-be crooked election officials know what would happen to them if they undertook to repeat their operations of 1902 and 1904. Public opinion is the best remedy for the situation which faces the Dominion to-day.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to take a few minutes of the time of the house in order to make a statement in regard to the second reading of this bill. The members in this comer of the house believe in the principle of income taxation and we feel that at the present time the govern-

Income War Tax Act

ment is going a little too far in reducing the personal income tax to the extent that is proposed in this bill. In 1926, some three years ago, there was a general reduction in the income tax; the schedule was materially reduced all round and certain further exemptions were given. Last year another reduction was made and additional exemption granted. This year it is proposed still further to reduce the income tax and 'also to allow further exemptions. We in this corner of the house, remembering the fact that this is a war tax act and that the different war tax acts now in existence do not produce enough revenue to take care of the expenses incidental to the war, are of opinion that the government is going, as I stated before, a little too fast in the matter. We believe the government could well give consideration to reductions in taxation m other forms which would enure to the benefit of the consumer generally. The organized farmers of Canada believe in the income tax as a fair measure of taxation. I should like to read to the house a resolution passed by the Canadian Council of Agriculture at their session of April 4, 5 and 6 of last year, dealing with the income tax. The resolution reads.
Resolved that this council recognizing the continuing need for the maintenance of stnct economy in public expenditure and for reduction in the national debt, with its heavy burden of interest, urges the Dominion government to do everything possible to serve these ends,
alBe it further resolved that reductions in taxation, as they become possible, should take place by the reduction and removal of protective duties on imports in preference to the reduction of other indirect taxes but that the income tax ought to be maintained as one of the chiet sources of public revenue. The council is oi opinion that the reduction successively made in the income tax and the increase in exemptions have tended seriously to impair its equity and productivity whereas it ought to be rendered both more equitable in its incidence and more general in its application by progressive improvements in the assessment and collection of the tax. The council suggests that inquiry into the methods and machinery of income taxation in Canada and elsewhere should be conducted by the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation with a view to the adoption of such improvements.
So far as I am aware the question of taxation has not been referred to the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation, but I wish to state in a few words the position we are going to take on this bill. It is quite possible that the government may propose some amendments when the bill gets into committee. If those amendments are acceptable to us, we shall be delighted. If they are not acceptable to us, we desire to inform the house that while it is usual to accept the principle of a bill on the second reading, [Mr. Gardiner.l
we wish to reserve our right to see what further proposals tihe government may make, and if they make no further proposals, then we intend to vote against the bill on the third reading.

speechtext:
I want to take
this opportunity of saying a few words again about the present system of taxing incomes of corporations, making the corporation pay a tax and then making the individual receiving dividends from the same corporation pay another tax. I am not referring to the super taxes; I am referring only to the normal taxes. We had this question up for discussion last year, but we could not make any impression on the minister. As a matter of fact, my own idea is that- the present system is very bad for business in this country, because if a man makes an investment in a business corporation he knows that not only will the profits of the company be taxed, but that afterwards any dividends he may receive from the company will also be taxed. The argument has been made that an investor receiving an income from one of the large prosperous corporations like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for instance, ought to pay income tax on his dividends even though the railroad company has already paid a tax on its profits. But consider how it works out in the case of a new company. We will say that a number of people are considering getting together and putting up their money for the purpose of starting a new business. They are met at once with this difficulty, that if the business is not a success they lose their money; if it is a success, then the joint stock ' company, under section two of this bill, will be called upon to pay income tax upon its profits, and afterwards the individual stockholder will also have to pay income tax on the dividends he receives. Considering the application of this tax in connection with an old established company rather beclouds the issue, but I want to submit that double taxation is a vicious principle, and it can never be defended. It prevents many people from going into new enterprises, because if the enterprise is not a success they lose their money, and if it is a success the government steps in and taxes them twice, once on the profits of the company and again on the dividends the stockholders receive. It is too late, I sup-

Income War Tax Act
pose, to have any change made this year, but I want to reiterate what I said last year, that I am sure it is a bad principle. All I suggest is that the individual holder of company stocks should be exempt from the normal tax on the dividends he receives from companies which themselves are paying a tax on their profits.

In the United States I
understand that there is no double taxation of this kind. There, I am instructed, the business tax is charged. It is somewhat higher than in this country, but the individual stockholder is not charged income tax a second time upon the revenues of the company. That, I understand, is correct, is it not? That being the case, I think it is wise, as the hon. member for Argenteuil has pointed out, that we should carefully consider whether we are not in that respect doing an injustice to the Canadian stockholder. It means that in many cases the foreign resident can invest in and control Canadian enterprises simply because he is not paying in Canada a second tax upon the income of that Canadian corporation which is exacted from the Canadian resident who is also a stockholder in the company. Foreign residents are obtaining control of a large proportion of the natural resources of this country. When the democratic party in the United States had their last convention they passed a resolution, a copy of which I have in my office, urging that as a national policy the financial men of the United States should obtain control in the neighbouring foreign countries of all those sources of supply of natural products which are necessary to the promotion of industry in the United States. The United States Department of Commerce, through its present very able secretary, Mr. Hoover, has time and time again urged upon the financial interests of that country that they should go out into the world, and particularly into Canada and Mexico, and obtain control of the sources of supply of those natural products which are necessarily imported into the United States for the promotion of American industry. They have done so in this country to a very large extent. At the present time the Americans control the great bulk of our asbestos production, in which, except for South Africa, we have practically a monopoly. They have control of our nickel production. They have control of the chief industries on this Ottawa river. They control the pulp and paper industry, and they control what is one of the great natural products of this country, hydro electric power along the river. They are acquiring control of hydro electric powers in
56103-117J
other sections of Canada, and they are using the control they exercise over companies in Canada for the purpose of preventing the carrying of the raw products of Canada through the various processes of manufacture in Canada, inasmuch as they control those raw products from their sources. They export them to the United States and use them there in the manufacture of goods which they send back into Canada for consumption. It is not a question of a protective tariff. I do not know just how we could meet it by an export tax without retaliation from the United States, but we should not encourage that process by taxing the Canadian stockholder in such industries twice while the American, who is carrying our raw products across the border to supply American industry, is free from double taxation in Canada. If the government will obtain the statistics which are available to them of the gradually increasing control which the Americans are obtaining of our raw products for manufacture, they will see that some advantage should be given by reducing the double tax on Canadians, which will induce the Canadian investor to invest more of his money in the stock of Canadian companies which are producing the raw materials in Canada. I do not know whether I have made myself clear, but the matter is really a serious one.
I know that some hon. gentlemen smile when I refer to some eight or nine years experience in Mexico, but the control by American financiers of the sources of raw material in Mexico has resulted in Mexico becoming a source of supply for other countries, and nearly the whole population of Mexico, dealing with the people generally, are simply receiving ordinary labourers' wages, while the people of other countries are enriched by converting those raw materials into manufactured articles. And that is going on in Canada, Mr. Chairman. I do not wish to deal with it now, perhaps next session I may do so, but I regard it as a matter most prejudicial to the interests of this country, and one that must be considered and met. Our financial men are buying back from foreign countries Canadian bonds which we might well sell abroad, and they are taking their money out of Canadian companies because of the double taxation which we exact from Canadian stockholders.

Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue will give us his idea on the subject, he having had a lot to do with the collection of this taxation.
