I appreciate very fully the arguments advanced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). But I should like to make a correction. He is not entirely right with regard to the exemption of the American shareholder from double taxation. I am informed that in the case of incomes of $5,000 and over the dividends of the American shareholder are taxable just the same as in Canada; in fact more so, because in Canada as a result of protests that were made against double taxation, we did establish what is known as the family corporation, which I think has given a good deal of relief.
That is correct.
On the other hand, the American corporation is taxed 13J per cent against our 8 per cent.
I admit that.

Perhaps a change should be made later on, but I do not like to speak definitely in the absence of the Minister of Finance. However, so far as this taxation is concerned, it is not very much to the disadvantage of the Canadian taxpayer.
I admit that the corporation tax in the United States is slightly higher than ours.
Five and a half per cent higher.

There is a measure before congress now I believe to reduce it, but still it will be in excess of our own. But that is an inducement to the American company to reincorporate a branch in Canada. That is the advantage which induces them to do so. 'Then, having established their business as a [DOT]Canadian corporation, the American shareholders of Canadian companies are placed in a much better position than the Canadian stockholders of similar companies.^ I do not wish to be dogmatic or assertive, but I regard this matter as one which must be considered in view of the fact that year by year the sources of supply of our mineral, pulp, and timber and other raw products are coming under American control. The Americans control the product from the time it is produced in Canada in the rawest form until they send it right across the border into their own factories and by various processes of manufacture enhance its value ten, twenty, even one hundred times; then they send the manufactured products back to us, having given employment in the meantime to American labour at the expense of Canadian labour. I am not discussing this in a party sense, I

am not discussing the tariff, but I am calling attention to a program endorsed by a great political convention in the United States and urged by the Secretary of Commerce of the United States time and again in official pronouncements, of which I have copies but not with me to-night. That policy has been urged upon American financiers as necessary in order to sustain for the future the various manufacturing industries of the United States which, having exhausted or partly exhausted their own sources of supply of raw materials have now to depend upon Mexico to the south and Canada to the north. It is a very serious question, and I think the double taxation of Canadian shareholders affects it very materially. I am not protesting against the measure,
I am simply in all sincerity calling it to the attention of the government.

Mr. Chairman, if the government are considering seriously the alteration of this double taxation at the next session, I should like to put forward another argument why I think it is a mistake. Take a Canadian with money to invest. We all agree that it should be invested in this country. He has to consider whether he will invest the money in a company or put it into bonds. If he puts it into bonds he has only one tax to pay. But let us assume that a dozen of us here were considering taking stock in a company. Each one of us naturally would say to himself; if we go into this company together, and it makes profits, the company will have to pay income tax on those profits, and then each of us personally will have to pay income tax on our individual share of those profits; perhaps we had better put our money into bonds. I submit for the minister's consideration whether it dots not militate against the development of our own resources by Canadians who have money to spare for investment.

W'ith regard to this proposed reduction, one would think that the income tax, which is almost the only tax by which revenue is raised in a direct way, would be fostered by the government of any country so that it might be paid by those best able to pay. Britain gives us a very good example in this line. She has been long populated to the limit, and she has had to calculate very closely the incidence of taxation. She believes that the place to look for revenue is where the money is, and not to try to collect it from those who are on the verge of penury, as is the case to-day with many of the agriculturists and wage earners of this country. In Britain it is a penny up or a penny down in the

Income War Tax Act
pound, according as the needs and circumstances of the country call for an advance or a reduction in the income tax. The policy of our government, it seems to me, is avowedly to put a line of cleavage more clear and distinct than ever between the idle rich and the wage earners. The same conditions apply at the present time as when the income tax was first imposed. The class for whom the war debt was incurred, that is the war profiteers, is now getting out of paying its just share, while the man who bore the brunt of battle and had to face death in the trenches is still to be taxed on his necessaries in order to furnish tax-free bonds for this same class. Moreover, he must still submit, when he purchases the necessaries of life, to prices above all comparison with those charged in other countries. Nothing is done by the government to lower the cost of living, but a substantial reduction is again made in favour of those who skyrocketed prices during the war.
Agriculture is in bad shape to-day in Canada. The farmers have had to submit to having their products set at about 50 per cent of the value which they should bear in comparison with the prices which were skyrocketed by every other concern producing in Canada during those years of anguish. Those concerns fixed their prices without let or hindrance and ran this country into debt to the tune of about two billions. So bad did the Liberal party consider the profiteering which then took place that in 1915 they insisted upon an investigation by the public accounts committee, and the scandal in connection with horses, surgical supplies, binoculars, bicycles, shovels, motor trucks and so forth, forms the subject of a pamphlet which I think Canada should blush to read at this time. This booklet is entitled "The War Contracts Scandal'' and was published by the central information office of the Canadian Liberal party. It is dated Ottawa, May, 1915. And these very men whose doings were investigated are, in this budget, relieved of the payment of their just share of what I might well term their ill-gotten gain. The supplies were purchased or were not purchased-no one knows. One of the first things complained of was a bill for over 81,000,000 which, without even an order in council, was incurred for goods which were supposed to have been purchased. Those who made these war fortunes are now to be relieved of income tax, while the farmer who had to be content with a set price on wheat during those years is still to be fleeced for the sake of that one class in the country.
Adam Smith once made a statement which will bear repetition to-day:
Ihe subjects of every state ought to contribute towards the support of the government as nearly as possible in proportion to their respective abilities; that is, in proportion to the revenue which they respectively enjoy under the protection of the state.
This principle cannot be challenged, though it is customarily ignored and violated by governments beholden to the specially privileged for their retention of power.
Even the large daily newspapers have commented upon this feature of the budget and some of them have spoken against this action taken by the government. The organized farmers of western Canada have long advocated the income tax as one of thei means of direct taxation for raising the revenue of the country, and the organ of the United Farmers of Alberta has lately come forward with this statement against such class discrimination :
The reduction of the income tax by a further 10 per cent on personal income and from 9 to 8 per cent on corporations, as announced by the Finance Minister in the House of Commons last week, is a starkly reactionary feature of the budget. . . The reductions in the income tax are discriminatory against the great body of Canadian citizens, and in a special sense in favour of a small body of citizens who are fortunate in having very large incomes-in favour of the class, in fact, who provide most of the campaign funds of the political parties. The estimated revenue from customs dues for the newT fiscal year is $153,600,000; the estimated revenue from income tax $55,300,000. The former duties are paid by every family in the Dominion, not in proportion to their ability to pay, but in proportion to their purchases. The head of an average family in Canada, whether he be farmer, wage worker, or business or professional man of moderate means, pays a far larger sum yearly into the federal treasury through customs duties than in income tax.
This means that every struggling wage earner pays taxes on his necessaries of life, skimping his wife and family of those necessaries in order to swell the coffers of the profiteers, those who are responsible for the great burden of debt which we now have hanging over our head. The policy of this government is not to place a tax on those best able to pay it, but to find the easiest means to filch the earnings of workers in a way in which they hope they may not be caught.
No notice seems to have been taken of the protest from this corner of the house. The government smiles to-day in stoic complacency, born of a feeling of security in the knowledge of the helplessness of the class which we in this comer of the house represent.

the taxation it is likely to meet in this Dominion. Therefore I say I have no sympathy with the argument of the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George. The man who has an income sufficient to bring him under the provisions of the Income Tax Act certainly should make his contribution. Sometimes it is said that the farmers of the west are protesting against income tax reduction because they do not pay the income tax. There is a mighty good reason why they do not pay income tax; it is because they have not sufficient income to do so. Therefore I am taking this point of view on the general principle of income tax- that any further reductions made by this government, or any government, will be bitterly opposed by the representatives and the members from the west. The whole sentiment of the west is against it. The people out there realize that if that source of revenue is removed and has to be made up again it will certainly be done at their expense. For that reason we are very sorry indeed to see the reduction that has been made, and we do hope that we will get some clear cut expression from the Minister of Finance now while we are on this matter as to what the intentions of the government are for the future.

I would like to ask the minister, before this clause passes, whether in its amended form it will impose a tax on the income of the wheat pool. If it will not apply to that organization, why is not the law so amended that the wheat pool, which is one of the most profitable organizations in Canada, will pay its fair share of income tax?

The proposed legislation will not make any change with regard to the liability of the wheat pool. What that liability is we are not absolutely certain. As my hon. friend, who is a lawyer, knows, the matter is at present sub judice; it is in the courts.
If there has been any doubt about it in the past why should we not amend the law so as to make it apply clearly and definitely in this case?
My hon. friend surely would not want us to amend the law in this case because we had to go to court to establish the validity of the law in some other matter.

The minister is amending the law so as to reach a whole class of people who, it is alleged, have escaped taxation in the past. Now if the wheat pool has up to the present escaped taxation, and there is a doubt whether
[Mr. Glen. [
the law applies to them, why not make the necessary amendment, particularly as the minister is dealing with a large class of persons who, it is alleged, are escaping taxation?
The wheat pool do not make any profit. They are a group of farmers engaged in selling their own products.

There is no corporation in
this country that is making a profit in that sense. The wheat pool makes its profit and distributes it amongst its members. That is exactly what occurs in any organization, whether incorporated or unincorporated.

For several years we
have heard the argument here that the corporation income tax is too high and that it is keeping capital out of the country. I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Cahan) in that regard. Evid-enly because of the fact that our corporation income tax is lower than it is in the United States, we are getting more capital from that country than our hon. friends seem to want to come in from that source. That is another huge bubble that has burst with a huge crack. I should like to say with regard to the wheat pool that there are no profits made in that organization at all. It consists of a number of farmers who have joined together in a co-operative way to sell the product of their labour, and all they get out of the wheat pool is the price received for the wheat after it has been sold. They make no profit at all. Therefore the wheat pool is not in the same position as a corporation which manufactures goods and makes a profit in its business. Cooperative organizations in the old country have been exempt from income taxation because of the fact that they are nonprofitmaking concerns. Probably the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has not yet had the opportunity of studying how these pools are organized and how they work, but if he has any idea in his head that the wheat pool is liable or should be liable for income taxation, I should like him to inform himself properly on the subject.

There is a difference
between the United Grain Growers and the wheat pool. The United Grain Growers, handling wheat as they do, make profits and do pay income tax. The wheat pool is an entirely different kind of organization, and handling wheat as it does without any profits it is entirely out of the question that it should be considered as coming within the range of taxation.

minister whether there has been any collection of arrears of income tax during last year, and if so what the amount is?

I want to say a word on
behalf of those engaged in farming and ranching in this country in connection with the operation of the income tax as it is at present. These men are engaged in a business the profits from which are largely determined by conditions over which they have no control, very largely climatic conditions. They may incur heavy losses for a period of years, and then the following year may make a profit on which they must pay income tax, although that profit is in no case sufficient to cover the losses they sustained in previous years. I think a good many cases of actual hardship are occuring under the act as it is at present drawn and administered, and I should like to urge the minister to take into serious consideration the question of changing the income tax so that the assessment of profits may be made on the basis of three years operations at least. In connection with the question of income tax, I should like to present to the house a resolution passed at the annual convention of the Western Live Stock Growers. It reads as follows:
Whereas agriculture and its attendant industry of live stock production represent the basic industry of this Dominion and as such require the greatest attention and development and expansion;
And whereas taxation of income under the provisions of the Income War Tax Act is based on annual net profit or gratuity;
And whereas this method of taxation on a yearly return is inequitable and detrimental to the advancement of agriculture and live stock production for the following reasons,-
(a)	That production of live stock as to quantity and quality is dependent upon climatic conditions.
(b)	The annual expense of live stock production is often made excessive by adverse climatic conditions.
fc) The annual profit of production of live stock is controlled largely by climatic as well as by market conditions.
(d)	That an annual conversion of the live
stock product into cash is frequently impossible.	.
(e)	That frequently several years of excessive yearly costs are experienced between the year of production and the year of marketing the live stock product.
(f)	That the profit on conversion of the live stock product into cash in any one year is frequently the result of two or more years of preparation and expenditure.

Therefore be it resolved that the Dominion government be asked to change its present method of determining taxable income so that from the taxable income for any one year there shall be deducted the net loss if any for the immediately preceding three year period.
That resolution is exactly in line with the request which I have already made to the minister.
Before I sit down I should like again to make the suggestion which I made in the debate on the budget, namely, that the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation should be authorized or instructed to inquire very carefully into the proposal which is made by the live stock producers that the assessment of income tax should be based on a period covering three or fouir years' operation. The present method is certainly working a distinct hardship on many men who are engaged in different branches of agriculture. It may be urged that this change should extend to other businesses as well. I am not prepared to express an opinion on that; I am conversant only with the agricultural industry, and I certainly think, so far as it is concerned, a change in the act is highly desirable and would be much more in the interest of the country than this continual reduction year after year in the rates of payment under the Income Tax Act.

They may be registered as to principal and it would be easy to make a return on that, but it is manifestly impossible for a municipality whose bonds are always issued to bearer to give the department any information.

I quite agree with the hon.
member's statement that there will be great difficulty, in obtaining all the information we would like to have. But by this we intend to get the power to make these inquiries and to secure information so far as we can. As the act stands now, in the case of dividends or salaries paid to employees that information must be given to the department.
And very exact information.

Very good; but we also
suspect, in fact we know that in many cases incomes are received by way of, we will say, interest or annuities, or something of that sort, which are never reported to the department. As the law stands now we have no authority to compel people to disclose information which might enable us to collect the tax, and we are taking the authority to enable us to oblige people to give us such information as we may desire. If the department suspects that in certain quarters the information is not being supplied as it should be, this will at least give us the power to secure that information if it is at all possible to get it. The hon. member will admit that, while this will not enable us to get all sources of income we might like to get, we shall at least have some power and authority to get something more than we are getting now.

That is a confession of
weakness at the start.

If the hon. member can
suggest some other method of making the clause more complete and certain, I should be glad to have it.

The first part of subsection 5 of section 7 reads:
All persons in whatever capacity acting, making payment of -interest, royalties, rents, annuities, compensation, remuneration or other fixed or determinable amounts, such as interest upon bonds, mortgages, deeds of trust or other similar obligations-
-shall be compelled to make a return. But the second part provides that:
All persons in whatever capacity acting-

And so on.
-making	payments under contracts,
whether written or verbal, relating to the buying and selling and otherwise dealing in stocks, bonds, debentures, mortgages, hypothecs, and other similar securities-
-shall also make a return. Does that mean that every stockbroker who buys or sells stocks under a verbal or written order shall report to the government all such purchases and sales?
No.

I admit that the language
must perhaps be broad in order to cover all the minister has in mind, but I should like him to tell us what he has in mind.

Generally speaking, what we are endeavouring to obtain is this. In the case of brokers dealing in stocks and bonds and who are making, as we know, profits which we have not been able to get at, who have a systematic scheme of making profits, we shall have authority to go in and obtain the information to tax them. It is not intended that they shall make a report of every individual sale or purchase they make. There might be a hundred or more a day, and it would be impossible.

Are we to infer that the
bond dealers are not making proper returns of their incomes?

No, it is the bond dealer's
customer who may be in the business of buying and selling stocks through a broker until it has become practically his vocation, his main source of income. It is not the man who just makes an occasional profit by buying and selling of stock and bonds.

Would the minister
kindly elucidate the reporting which is required under the first part of this clause? How far would he put that into effect? As the Minister knows, there are already in vogue two systems of reporting, one in England, where the payor deducts a given rate of income tax, and the other in the United States, where the report is made by the payor to the government and income tax assessed on that by the government. In Canada there seems to be no reporting except in the case of salaries, dividends, directors' fees, and that sort of thing, which are easily ascertainable. It occurs to me that the minister is broadening this clause so that all income will have to be reported. Will the minister kindly elucidate that?

It is intended to give the
minister fairly wide powers. I do not think * it is the intention to make everybody report.
The clause says, "on such forms and at such times as the minister may prescribe." The minister is not going to be unreasonable in this matter, but where he has reason to think that it is advisable in the interests of the revenue, he can demand these returns. He might perhaps fix a certain amount. This clause at least gives the minister power to demand these returns, but of course, it is not intended to use that power in any unreasonable wray.

The difficulty with the Canadian income tax is that it is not enforced. I think if the minister is going to make a provision for reporting, it should be watertight and everybody who makes payments should have to report, or else leave it alone; and the same in regard to bond coupons; the reporting should be complete, or leave it alone.	.

Is the hon. member advocating that in every instance the department should insist upon these reports being made? He speaks of making it watertight. Does he mean that we should exercise no discretion whatever in the matter, but insist upon every one of the persons here indicated making a report? I am simply trying to get the idea of the hon. member.

I am asking the minister what is in his mind. If I make a payment to a man, and it involves a profit, am I to report it? If so, has every payment of the kind to be reported. I think we are letting ourselves in for a great deal of trouble here. The enforcement of the income tax is the greatest problem relating to the income tax to-day. I do not think we should criticize very much the reduction in the income tax, if that reduction results in an increase in income, but when you come to thJ reporting I think you should either adopt it completely or leave it alone.

Something is left to the
discretion of the minister, and if he does not insist on as complete a system of reporting as the house thinks there should be, I have no doubt that he will be subjected to criticism at the next session.

Is not the objection of the hon. member for Toronto East Centre this, that you are placing it in the control of the minister to discriminate as between those who will make returns? This clause allows the minister or the officers of his department to select a certain few. They may take the men on a certain list and enforce the provision as against them, while it is not generally enforced. It seems to me that the burden

of the complaint of the member for Toronto East Centre is that you should state specifically the nature of the returns you require, and from whom they are required, and then make every person of that class make such a return, and make it applicable throughout the whole country to similar classes or persons. This section is not to apply to the broker at all, as explained by the minister. It is not to get at the broker who is escaping making a proper return. As far as the brokerage firms in this country are concerned, the minister has power now to make a thorough examination of all the books of these firms, and I have known it done time and again in the city of Montreal. What the minister is asking for here is for a return of all payments, "under contracts, whether written or verbal, relating to the buying and selling and otherwise dealing in stocks, bonds, debentures, mortgages, hypothecs, and other similar securities." I do not see why that should apply to the buying and selling of securities, any more than it should apply to the buying and selling of land, or the buying and selling of wheat, or any other commodity, but if the provision is to be that every contract relating to the buying and selling of these classes of stocks and securities shall be reported to the minister, then make the provision general so that every person who enters into contracts of that kind shall make a report, and do not allow the minister to prescribe the forms in his own discretion, and to select the people whom he is going to compel to make these returns and pay a tax on the contracts to which reference is made in this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I point out to my hon.
friend that the minister now has those powers which he objects to. He has power to demand, for instance, that all salaries be reported, but he does not ask my hon. friend to report the salaries of the employees of his household. He exacts, under the power he has, the information from the large employers of labour.

I make a return for my
employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The most satisfactory source
of collection as regards income tax is from the salaries, because under the act the large employers of labour are compelled to report the salaries they are paying, and companies paying dividends are compelled to report the dividends they are paying, and the department has power to audit the books to see that a

proper return is made. But a certain latitude is allowed the minister because he must use reasonable discretion and not go after small employers of labour, for instance, and small concerns. This is intended to get after those who, we are satisfied from experience, are evading taxation.
What class of people are you getting after?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From time to time the attention of the department may be directed to the fact that systematic attempt is being made to evade the income tax. We have had no complaint with regard to the powers the minister now has to demand information as to salaries, which powers are as wide as those now sought.

Is it the intention of the minister under this clause to exact from small mortgagors returns of the interest payments they make? A firm of solicitors may be handling a thousand mortgages for perhaps fifty clients, involving periodical payments. Is it the intention to require everyone of those mortgagors to make out a return? If so, I see a little rebellion in some parts of the country.

I do not care to make any definite commitment in regard to it, but I would say that in a general way it is not the intention to persecute people. In the case of many of these small amounts the chances are that we would not ask for any information at all. We might perhaps fix a minimum amount to be reported. I admit, Mr. Chairman, that we are asking that the minister be given fairly wide discretionary powers, and that you have to trust him to use those powers in a wise way. He has similar powers under several other statutes. I think it is perfectly proper that these discretionary powers should be given to him.
